facts.fact: The kingdom is Hemkot; its capital is Taravan; the far valley is Neshar; the pass is the Shilak Pass; the last village below it is Kothi Shilak.
Heroine of Book 1 is Meera, 29, smuggler-guide and secret leader of the crew the wardens call the Salt Fox.
Hero of Book 1 is Rohan, 35, captain of the queen's pass-wardens on the Shilak side.
Kiran, 24 in Book 1, is Meera's younger brother and calls her Didi when afraid.
Ila, 30 in Book 1 and 31 in Book 2, is Rohan's younger sister and a crown pass-surveyor.
Kunal, 32 in Book 1 and 33 in Book 2, is prince of Neshar, nephew of Regent Pritam, and secret leader of the hill council rebels.

In winter the jogini let only rope-bound pairs cross a closed pass alive. Binding requires one hand-spun wool rope, the same knot tied on each other's wrist at a jogini cairn, and each speaking name and destination.
Ropes longer than twelve arm-spans are refused. Meera's red rope is eight arm-spans.

A bound pair cannot separate beyond the rope's length, tied or not, until meltwater first runs at the cairn where they were bound. Beyond the length both lose heat fast; at about twice the length the path vanishes and the mountain takes them.

Each lie to one's bound partner costs body heat in proportion to how much the truth would change the partner's choices. Small lie: white fingertips for an hour. Middling: frostnip and a night's shaking. Great: frostbite and dead flesh. A lie about the partner's life or death kills.
Silence, evasion, refusal, obvious jokes, lies to others and truths are free. Fire does not warm lie-cold.
A promise made while bound, if broken while still bound, strikes the breaker as a great lie.
Loophole: the partner lied to can take the lie-cold onto their own skin by touch; they then know a lie was told and its size, but not the truth, and they pay the cold themselves.
Bound pairs see the winter line marked by faint blue cairn-light at night. Armies cannot cross; only pairs bind, one pair per rope.
The Shilak Cairn's stones hum in wind and ring when a lie is told inside the ring.

The Closing Law, written 60 winters before Book 1, forbids crossing a high pass between first snow and first thaw on pain of hanging. Wardens cannot pardon; only the queen can. Sharing a fire with an unlawful crosser is harbouring, also a hanging crime.
A crown writ of passage signed by the queen's own hand makes a winter crossing lawful. Anyone named on it enters the Closing Roll and owes winter service for life.
The queen's seal is a lapis stone cut with a mountain goat. Rohan carries it in his coat; it must be pressed before the Neshar assembly at the Snow Fair to revoke Regent Pritam's claim.
Meera carries twelve packets of redbark powder for the grey cough in Ranu. The crates bore a crown stamp that had been scraped off.
Rohan carries the clean-cut end of Dilan's rope in his coat.
Meera keeps waxed ledgers she calls the count, recording every person and packet carried and every price.
Meera's red rope was spun from wool sold by Lata's house in Taravan.
Rohan has twenty days from the start of Book 1 to reach the Snow Fair.
Jassi, 40, Meera's goat handler and second, dies in the avalanche in Book 1 chapter 3. He stays dead.
In Book 1 chapter 26 Meera loses the ring and little fingers of her left hand to one great lie about Kiran. Permanent.
Kiran has a frostbitten ear from the crossing on which Dilan died, two winters before Book 1.
Dilan, 23, Rohan's youngest warden, died two winters before Book 1 after cutting his own rope to keep Kiran from being dragged off the ice.
Varun, 38, Rohan's lieutenant, is Regent Pritam's man. He chose the approach route, set off the avalanche and sells stolen crown redbark to Meera's crew through a middleman.
The Rope-Hut is a stone shelter below the Long Saddle on the far side, with one chulha, one sleeping shelf and a limited juniper woodpile.
The Long Saddle is the high snowfield of the Shilak Pass, two days across.
Ranu is the fever village in lower Neshar; its healer is Nimmi, 50.
Garh Neshar is the regent's seat with a brass assembly bell; the Snow Fair is held on the frozen river meadow below it.
Rohan has hanged two lowland smugglers in three winters and seized Meera's crew's loads twice. He secretly pays poor families' seizure fines from his wage.
Meera charges rich clients double so poor ones cross free.
Asha, 28 in Book 1, leads a rival smuggler crew from the lower salt road and is paid by Varun to track the seal in Book 1.
Tej, 43 in Book 1, is Regent Pritam's general. He refuses the order to fire Ranu in Book 1 chapter 27 and is exiled after the Snow Fair as the regent's man.

Lata, 40 in Book 1, widowed wool trader of Taravan. Her husband Mohit died of fever in Neshar four winters before Book 1. She and Tej loved each other young; his soldiers burned her family's wool sheds in the Neshar Rising, 20 winters before Book 1.
Queen Sarala, 61, rules Hemkot, ill but alive. Book 1 is the 30th winter of her reign.
Regent Pritam, 51, regent of Neshar and Kunal's uncle, plans to be invested as ruler at the Snow Fair on the claim that the queen is dying.
The Old Bargain: founders Saro (a warden) and Hemi (a smuggler) first crossed Shilak bound about 300 winters ago. The original price was a promise; the crown later recast it as a death.
The last Bargain payment, 60 winters before Book 1, was Rohan and Ila's grandfather, a warden who walked into the snow. The Closing Law was written the next spring.
The Shilak Cairn's inner face is carved with two hands bound by one rope. The Under-Cairn carving reads 'carried till no thaw'.
Asha ties every knot in her grandmother's pattern, which matches the cairn carving and is Hemi's knot.
At Book 1's thaw the jogini warn through the cold that the Old Bargain is unpaid and the pass will close forever after the fourth winter unless someone pays.
Book 1 ends with Meera and Rohan retying an ordinary rope by choice after the bond ends, as their betrothal, and drafting the Winter Crossing Law.
Rohan's form of address for Meera is Guide; hers for him is Captain, until it changes.
Kunal is the masked buyer who pays for Ranu's medicine in Neshar silver stamped with a cut corner.
The queen's seal wax is mixed with her own blood, proof she sealed it herself.
Roop and Chand are the last crew pair to cross back from Ranu, bound to each other until the thaw. Roop carries Kiran's note.
Jassi names his pack goats Pomegranate, Auntie, Sheriff, Magistrate and Judge.
Wardens make a sweep of Kothi Shilak every tenth day, so Meera expected a patrol on the day Rohan arrives.
The brass button left as the token for the next drop is small, domed, plain and brand new with a stiff shank. The next courier is to carry its twin, and without the twin no crate is released.
Kiran's note gives Nimmi's tally as forty-one sick, nine of them under ten, and six buried.

The Closing Law notice is nailed to the left gatepost of Kothi Shilak, and the hanging tree is a deodar just outside the gate with one peg hammered into the trunk per hanging. Two pegs are pale from last winter.
Meera, with Bindu's help, hides the redbark in the middle of one of Bindu's raw wool bales. They have rehearsed this for four winters.
Hakam is the three-fingered old man of Kothi Shilak whom Meera points out in the yard.
Rohan's party for the crossing is two wardens (Rohan and Varun) and two guides (Jassi and Meera); the other wardens return to the post.
Rohan has told Varun, and no one else beyond the queen, that he carries the queen's seal.
Wardens carry an iron probe spike used to find salt in grain; the salt house wool bales were probed to arm's depth with it but not cut open.
Varun's coat has one new brass button among pewter ones; he claims a pedlar sold it to him after he lost a button on the stair.
Widow Puja's seizure fine is eighteen silver, for salt found in her late husband's lean-to; Rohan pays it secretly.
Meera tells the yard her mother died of the grey cough ten winters ago because medicine was on the wrong side of the law.
The warden report of Dilan's death records blood on the ice and a curl of frozen cartilage no longer than a fingernail, which Rohan reads as the rim of an ear.
Rohan knows a warden who lets a known load cross is harbouring it by the letter of the Closing Law; he writes no report and decides to follow the redbark toward the Salt Fox.
The wool bales (Bindu's, with the hidden redbark) stand in the goat pen beneath the salt house; the wardens search the pen last.

Badami is Jassi's old bell-goat, too old for crossings, left in the salt-house pen. Jassi carries her kid-days bell on a thong at his collar; she is to retire with him to his sister's orchard of forty apricot trees.
Meera takes Badami's small dented brass kid-bell from Jassi's fist and keeps it buttoned in her coat with Kiran's note.
Rohan has two or three cracked ribs on his left side and cannot raise his left arm above the shoulder.
Of the five pack goats, Pomegranate and Auntie are dug out dead; the other three are never found. All the wardens' probes and tent poles are lost or left behind.
Rohan believes Varun was buried in the slide and is dead; Meera heard an iron ring before the first crack but has not interpreted it.
Meera gave Rohan odds: about one in four the gully slides, one in three the face cornice; Varun chose the gully as the lesser risk.
The twelve redbark packets are small palm-sized bundles of waxed paper tied with thread, laid in three rows of four inside the oilcloth roll at the bottom of Meera's pack.
Meera and Rohan bet on whether he can stay silent for an hour; the stake is the loser's sattu at the next halt, which Rohan wins and will collect then.
A waystone stands at the foot of the climb to the Long Saddle: a squat grey pillar with a shelf of flat stones left by earlier crossers. Meera builds a three-stone cairn there for Jassi.
Because Meera's fingertips are white from the demonstration lie for an hour, Rohan notes they cannot testify to anything she says during that hour.
The shelf at the waystone hides a cache of old dried dung cakes under the lowest slab, left by goat-crews for the next crossers; an unwritten mountain custom Meera knows.
Meera has carried two hundred and six people across the pass, not counting salt, and has written each in her ledger; she tells Rohan this number in the question trade.
The Shilak Cairn's two-hands-and-rope carving is also on the waystone's east face, worn smooth.
Meera and Kiran, as children, once played at the end of a rope and felt the rope's cold; their mother screamed.

The winter Meera was fifteen (fourteen winters before Book 1), on her first bound crossing with her mother, she went back for a dropped mitten a few paces past the rope's length and felt the rope's cold; her mother screamed. This replaces the earlier childhood-rope-play fact; Kiran is not part of the memory.

The waystone at the foot of the Long Saddle climb hums low in wind and rises in pitch, with its blue cairn-light thickening, when a lie is told to a bound partner nearby; it stays low and level at a true answer. This extends F015 beyond the Shilak Cairn.

The warden chronicle phrase, from the first chronicle of the Shilak post, reads: 'Two brothers in arms. They crossed the closed pass bound by one rope, and the pass has stood open to the faithful ever since.' Crews tell it as a warden and a smuggler.
Rohan hunted the Salt Fox crew for one winter because the law required it, and has hunted it two more winters for Dilan's sake; Meera notes the exact accounting.
Jassi's spare cord is a braided goat-hair line he used to tether kids; Meera carries it in her pack and uses it to bind Rohan's ribs.
Rohan's cracked ribs are the seventh and eighth on the left side; he also cannot raise the left arm above the shoulder (matches F068).
Rohan carries a grey warden-issue pattu, smelling of camphor, rolled at his belt; it survived the avalanche.

The ribs lie happens at first light on the pitch above the waystone; the pair shelter in a hollow under the Saddle's lip for the day and night, losing a day, and Meera shakes through the night. Nineteen of Rohan's twenty days remain.
Meera first calls Rohan by his given name here, unnoticed by her, while he calls her Meera at the end.

The ribs lie happens at first light on the pitch above the waystone, with seventeen of Rohan's twenty days remaining at that dawn. The pair shelter in a hollow under the Saddle's lip for the day and night, losing a day, so sixteen remain by the following night. Meera shakes through the night.

Rohan's writ is a folded creamy paper with red wax, carried in a boiled-leather writ case stamped with a goat. Meera cuts a strip from the case to make snow goggles, and Rohan moves the paper inside his coat.
Asha's crew is recognisable by packs covered in onion-skin ochre canvas.

The crew ledge is a shelf cut by Bindu's mother forty winters ago into the cornice on the south face, with iron pegs and a cache of three days' food and two dry blankets. It is reached across a gully with an eight-pace snow bridge.
Rohan tells Meera that he carries a thing the regent's side would pay a lordship for, and that he believes the four pursuers have been told where to find him. He declines to name it.
Meera infers from the two ropes that Asha's four are two bound pairs who each spoke their true names at the Shilak Cairn, and that someone paid them enough to do it.
Rohan wonders aloud who knew his route, saying it was chosen for him and only a handful saw it.
Meera tells a small lie to Rohan ('I don't care a fig for the shelf'); her right fingertips whiten for an hour and Rohan reads it from her hand.
The Rope-Hut has a sprig of juniper nailed above its door and a door facing downhill; it lies about an hour's descent by cairn-light from the crew ledge on the south slope.
Asha's four, after losing the tracks on the bare ridge, cast east along the Saddle's lip rather than finding the ledge.
Meera hauls Rohan out of the gully with a sliding-grip two-to-one drag on the red rope anchored to her axe, which Bindu calls the lazy woman's lift.
The crown redbark wrappers carry a faint round sieve-mark pressed into the wax along the fold, from the lowland guild stores' silk sieve with a ring in the weave.
The regent's hunters announce themselves with a two-note falling horn call that Meera recognises, and they climb the Neshar-side road with torches in a long line of fourteen or more.
Dilan's rope end is a forearm's length of grey hand-spun wool, rolled and tied with a scrap of its own cord. One end is whipped with black thread (Dilan's own neat work); the other is the clean cut.
Rohan swore at the Shilak warden hall, before eleven wardens, with Dilan's rope end in his hand, to find the one who stood at its far end.
Dilan was bad at knots except the black-thread whipping, could not carry a tune, and sang a hymn every watch that he mistook for a love song.

Meera's firewood rule: one question each per night; a refusal burns one extra stick over the night's five. The hut holds thirty-six sticks at dusk of the first full day, enough for seven nights plus one.
Meera and Rohan decide to wait in the Rope-Hut a day while the regent's hunters camp under the Saddle's lip; the winter line meets the Neshar road at the third bend, half a day down.

Varun read the crossing party aloud at the post gate the night before: three wardens and two guides. Rohan struck the third warden's name at dawn, so only two wardens went into the gully. Meera heard this, so 'three wardens and two goat-folk' could only have come from the written plan.
Lalit is Asha's tracker, a thin young man bound to her by rope and carrying a spyglass. Asha's second pair stays at the camp, unnamed.
Asha gives Meera the whole day and the next until the light goes; after that she comes down with four.
Firewood count: thirty-one sticks after the first night, thirty after Rohan's first refusal, twenty-nine after the second.

Rohan knows the Neshar-side road from walking it as a boy with his father and from mapping the post's end of it. He names a herdsmen's cut above the third bend, behind a stone fold, and a shrine on the way.
Rohan has a lung fever with a rattling cough that has been building unspoken; it comes to a crisis at the end of chapter 10.

Firewood count (replaces earlier F110): thirty-one sticks in the bundle at the start of chapter 10's day; Meera takes the night's five (twenty-six left), then burns one stick for each of Rohan's two refusals (twenty-five, then twenty-four).

Revised: Varun read the crossing party over from his written sheet in the post room the night before, with the guides present: three wardens and two guides. Rohan struck the third name at dawn. So 'three wardens and two goat-folk' could only have come from the plan or someone in that room.

Meera deliberately withholds from Rohan that Asha's information came from the plan, because it came from his own post, she cannot yet rule him out, and it is leverage for Kiran's name. She notes that silence is free.

The queen's seal is a lapis stone about a thumb-joint long, threaded on a cord through a hole in its shoulder, tied off in a warden's double hitch (two turns round the standing part, a tuck, a locking half-turn), and sewn into a hidden pocket in the seam at the nape of Rohan's coat.
Meera's own habitual knot, taught by Bindu when she was five, is a flat reef with a half hitch; she unpicks it and ties the warden's double hitch instead.
Meera burns four sticks to boil the juniper pot and uses the hut's juniper sprig from above the door for the steam; the bundle is not recounted on the page.
The mountain goat appears on Hemkot's coins; the seal's goat is cut finer and differently.

A wind-felled juniper lies about ten paces downslope of the Rope-Hut door, just past the rope's eight-span reach from the sill; Meera burns its wet deadfall by day and saves the dry stick bundle for nights.

Asha's crew leaves a bundle hung in the deadfall juniper: sattu, dried apricots, a twist of salt and a strip of smoked goat, tied in the three-nested-loop knot that matches the cairn carving. Meera sketches it in the count and does not eat or decide its purpose yet.
Rohan takes a second half-pinch of redbark at first light this chapter; his fever has broken but he cannot walk.

The second man Rohan hanged was Ketan, seventeen, carrying forty pounds of salt to his mother in a high village; the first was an unnamed lowland runner of about thirty-one who carried powder for the regent's men. Rohan paid the mother's fine for the lean-to afterwards.
The Shilak post's file on the guides records only the high price of a crossing, not the double rate for the rich or the free crossings for the poor. Rohan has read it eleven times.

Asha's crew leaves a bundle hung in the deadfall juniper: sattu, dried apricots, a twist of salt and a strip of smoked goat, tied in the three-nested-loop knot that matches the cairn carving. Meera sketches it in the count as 'Same as cairn'. She eats a strip of the goat at noon; Rohan does not. She has not decided its purpose.

The second man Rohan hanged was Ketan, seventeen, a lowland boy from the Taravan road carrying forty pounds of salt over the closed pass to his mother, who had married into Neshar and had a cough. The first was an unnamed lowland runner of about thirty-one who carried powder for the regent's men. Rohan afterwards paid the fine the post levied on Ketan's mother.

Rohan's fallback route (the herdsmen's cut from the third bend behind the stone fold, past the shrine, round the spur to the Saddle's lip) was drawn at the post table two nights before the crossing, by Rohan with a ruler on a single copy in Varun's neat hand; only the two of them saw it.
Meera's rope signals: three short pulls mean halt, one long pull means come.

At dusk of this chapter the bundle holds nineteen dry sticks; five are burned for the night and a sixth for Meera's refusal, leaving thirteen. Nine days remain to the Snow Fair and they agree to move within two days.

Restates F127: the fallback route was drawn by Varun in his neat hand on a single copy at Rohan's direction, with Rohan holding the ruler. Rohan also named the cut aloud to Meera on the second night. Rohan rules Meera out as the seller because she has been tied to him every hour since.
Varun has been buried under the gully for about nine days.

Rohan's grandfather, an early warden of the Shilak post, went out in a night storm to check the cairns for a lost party and was found at the thaw; Rohan's father told it that way, and the Closing Law was written the next spring 'for him'. Rohan believes it was an accident.

The Goat's Teeth is a spine of steep rock on the south-east shoulder of the Long Saddle, with three ledges, two ropes' worth of down-climbing and an ice chimney, dropping to the Neshar side below the third bend. Jassi named it and hated it.
Firewood stands at twelve dry sticks after Rohan burns one for his silence about the fines, on the night of the hunters' climb.
Firewood stands at twelve dry sticks after Rohan burns one stick for his silence about the fines; Meera banks the coals and spends no sticks that night (thirteen at the end of ch13).

Rohan's grandfather was a warden of the Shilak post sixty winters ago, the winter before the Closing Law, before the post had a hall; he went out in a night storm to check cairns for a lost party and was found at the thaw. The law was written the next spring.
Rohan says he has buried seven wardens and that Pritam would open the Shilak to his grain wagons by midwinter if the Closing Law lapsed.

The Goat's Teeth is a spine of rock on the south-east shoulder of the Long Saddle with three ledges, two ropes' worth of down-climbing and an ice chimney, dropping to the Neshar side below the third bend; a pair needs a day and a half, Rohan one-armed about two. Jassi named it.

The regent's hunters came up the Goat's Teeth as two roped pairs (four men) via the ice chimney; neither Rohan nor Meera knows who told them the route. Meera notes every salt-road crew knows the Teeth.

Rohan breaks the sword-wrist of the second hunter and splints it with a scabbard and cloak strip; the first hunter is disarmed. Rohan leaves both in the lee of a rock on the second ledge with their cloaks.
Rohan keeps a thumb-length twist of crown-grade redbark from the first hunter's purse, with the guild's silk-sieve ring pressed in the wax; he sets it on the hearth for Meera at the hut.
Meera's hands are red, swollen and split across the knuckles from working bare on the Teeth (ordinary cold, not lie-cold); Rohan warms them against his bare right side.
A wind-slab tongue on the far shoulder of the chimney is cut by Meera with her axe adze and fills the chimney throat, blocking the second hunter pair for about the rest of the day.
The Rope-Hut door's oak bar breaks in the gust and the door tears open; the eleven remaining sticks, laid in a row by the wall beside the door, are swept out over the sill toward the felled juniper.

Meera lashes the broken Rope-Hut door bar with Jassi's goat-hair cord and wedges the door with her pack; they recover seven of the eleven dry sticks from the felled juniper's root plate, and four are lost downslope.
Meera's redbark supply uses a brass button as the token for each drop, and the courier carries its twin (matches F052/F060); Meera links it to Varun's new brass button.
Rohan names the thing the regent's side would pay a lordship for as the queen's seal and confirms Meera has held it; he had told only Varun and the queen.
Rohan says he suspected Meera was the Salt Fox after her 'you deliver me' in ch14 but chose not to know; he stood at Varun's wedding.
A sincere promise made while bound makes the rope hum a low, level note that Meera feels through her wrist; the sound stays even rather than climbing, as a true answer does at the waystone.
Rohan noticed on waking that the seal's cord was retied in the warden's double hitch, and wondered who taught Meera that knot.
Meera heard one clean iron strike on stone before the avalanche's first crack in ch3, and now recognises it as a pick set to start the slide, matching the hunters' picks on the Teeth.
The hunters came up the one chimney line of the Goat's Teeth that lets out behind the stone fold on the herdsmen's cut, the line drawn on Rohan and Varun's single fallback sheet.
Varun has been buried about eleven days at ch16 (revises the nine-day figure in F131).
Rohan noticed the seal cord was retied in his double hitch but snugged harder than he snugs it, which is why he wondered who taught Meera the hitch.
Meera wrote Lalit's called party number ('three wardens, two goat-folk') in the count; she shows the page to Rohan.
The Ranu graves lie in rows on the terraced slope above the village, cut into frozen ground; the smaller mounds are child-length and some carry toys or pine boughs.
Rohan counts thirty-one new graves; Nimmi says thirty-one died this winter, before midwinter.
Meera and Rohan leave the Rope-Hut by the winter line down the south slope to the Neshar road at the third bend, because the Goat's Teeth chimney is plugged by the slab.
Meera now calls Rohan by name when she wants to be heard, and tells him to walk behind her and uphill of her so he can anchor the rope.
Rohan splits his right knuckles on the herdsmen's stone fold in anger over Varun.
Sunni, seven, is a sick child in Ranu; her mother is unnamed. Other named sick: Hira the weaver (blue lip), Bholu's mother, old Lalli, the Dev boy and his father, Kamla's two small children.
A course of redbark is a pinch in hot walnut-leaf tea morning and night for three days; a packet is two courses (three if stretched). Nimmi can brew six cups at a time, so doses go out in waves.
The badge under Kiran's pillow is brass gone brown, palm-wide, stamped with the queen's goat head, with a small dent in the rim.
Meera now knows Kiran holds a warden's badge and withholds it from Rohan as a free silence; she does not yet know whose it is.
Sunni rings Badami's dented bell, which Meera lends her; Sunni dies holding it.
Three of the twelve redbark packets were ruined on the Goat's Teeth (two split along the fold, one damp-set like clay); nine sound packets at two courses each give eighteen courses.
Forty-one are sick in Ranu: eighteen get a course (Sunni last on the list, third water at dusk) and twenty-three do not.
Each trip to the nearest well (a hundred paces from Nimmi's house) takes Meera and Rohan about a quarter hour together, because the rope forces Meera to walk it with him; this delays the waters.

Meera opened only one packet before Ranu, for Rohan's lungs. Stock at Ranu: three packets ruined on the Teeth, eight whole packets (sixteen courses), the opened packet short two half-pinches (one course), and the hunter's crown-grade twist (F141, one course): eighteen courses. Thinning a dose 'turns nobody' (revises F162's 'three if stretched').
Forty-one sick in Ranu now matches Kiran's note: twenty-five have been buried since the note and twenty-five more have fallen sick, so the figure holds.

Every well person in Ranu is nursing, and the boy who hauled water for Nimmi fell ill the day before, so Meera and Rohan must haul water themselves; Rohan counts eleven well trips on the day Sunni dies and shares the guilt for the delay.

On first seeing Rohan, Kiran's eyes go to his face and he flinches before joking; he sleeps gripping Dilan's badge in his fist. Meera first reads this as ordinary smuggler fear of a warden (C16 clue).
Sunni's mother returns Badami's dented bell and Meera tells her to bury it with Sunni; the bell is buried with the child and Meera no longer carries it.
The regent's patrol wears grey wool with a small brass bell stitched on each shoulder; the captain has a red moustache and one soldier is called Pasang.
Nimmi's goat shed is a lean-to behind her house with three goats and a hay loft; the patrol marks its door with an ash handprint.
The patrol marks every sick house with a plate-wide ash handprint on the lintel, and says no one may go in or out of a marked house after the sixth day without a pass.
Nimmi estimates eight days until the Snow Fair if the road holds, with the general to ride up after it.
Four days remain to the Snow Fair at the end of ch19 (replaces F177's eight days, consistent with nine days at ch13 dusk). The general rides up after the Fair.
The patrol's pass rule: no one goes in or out of a marked house after the third day without a pass (replaces F176's sixth day), so it falls before the Fair.

Nimmi gives Meera and Rohan her storehouse, a plank room against the back wall of her house, full of sacks of dried walnut leaf, with a clay brazier, blankets and a lamp. It shares a wall with the room where Kiran lies.

Meera's count has a separate ruled-off line near the back reading 'Shilak closed. Three winters. By order.' with Nimmi's yearly death numbers under it. She writes Rohan's name beside it and adds 'Carried water, eleven trips.'
Meera mentioned in the Rope-Hut that the cold gets into her knuckles; Rohan remembers it and treats her split hands with goat fat from Nimmi's shelf.

Rohan's grey warden pattu is hidden at the bottom of a sack of walnut leaf in Nimmi's storehouse because the patrol seeks a man in grey; he wears Meera's spare brown pattu (with a hole in the hem), too short in the sleeves.

A grain carter allowed up the lower road with turnips told Nimmi that a crown surveyor woman has been kept in the Garh Neshar guest-house since first snow and has measured the yard, saying the north wall is two spans out of true.

Rohan concedes three days in Ranu; they leave at first light on the fourth day, with the Fair four days off at chapter start, one day on the road to Garh Neshar for a sound man and a day and a half for Rohan.
Meera agrees to walk the seal in beside Rohan to the Fair meadow in daylight, in front of the assembly; Rohan does not promise to forgo the writ at the thaw.
The hardest cases in Ranu get a second course; Meera says six days would be needed to treat everyone properly, and Nimmi can carry the remaining waves alone after the third day's dusk.
Rohan carries his draft assembly speech, written on the back of one of Nimmi's tally sheets, folded inside his coat beside Dilan's rope end; the blockade line is unwritten.

Revised: Rohan concedes two days in Ranu, not three. The Fair is four days off at chapter start; they leave at first light on the third day, and a day and a half of road puts them at Garh Neshar the evening before the Fair. The two marked cases take their last dose at dusk on the second day. Meera names the patrol's third-day pass rule (F179) as part of her cost: Nimmi must finish the waves behind a shut door.
Revised: Meera says six days would be needed to treat everyone properly; Nimmi carries the remaining waves alone after the second day's dusk.
When Rohan says 'I will not' (pull the rope at the second dusk), the rope hums low and level; Meera feels it, writes 'Two days. R. promised.' in the count and takes his hand (applies F149).

Recount after Kiran's day of sleep: the Fair is three days off at chapter start. Rohan concedes one day in Ranu; the two marked cases take their last dose at dusk tomorrow; they leave at first light the morning after; a day and a half of road lands them at Garh Neshar the evening before the Fair. Supersedes F185 and F189.

The patrol's pass rule bites on the third day, the day after Meera and Rohan leave, so Nimmi must finish the waves behind a shut door (consistent with F179). Meera says six days would treat everyone properly; Nimmi carries the remaining waves alone after tomorrow's dusk. Supersedes F187 and F190.
When Rohan says he will not pull the rope at tomorrow's dusk, the rope hums low and level; Meera writes 'One day. R. promised.' in the count and takes his hand. Supersedes F191's wording.
The woodpile where Kiran stops is behind Nimmi's goat shed, about ten paces from the storehouse door, within the rope's eight spans.
The initials 'DIL' are scratched with a nail point on the back of the badge; Kiran wore it on a string against his skin.

On the storm night Dilan caught Kiran on the Saddle's lip, roped them waist to waist to walk him down, and the ice shelf above the third bend gave way under Dilan. Dilan cut his own rope with his knife as it dragged Kiran toward the lip. Kiran lay on the ice until dawn, his ear frozen to the shelf, and walked home with the badge from the snow by his hand. Dilan's last words to him were 'sorry about the hymn.'
Meera has heard Dilan's name and the hymn story from Rohan before this chapter, and recognises the badge from it.
Meera refuses to promise Kiran silence because a promise made while bound would strike her as a great lie if broken; she offers silence, which is free.

Revises F197: on the storm night Kiran went up the Saddle alone with four loads of salt for the Dev people, lost the line within the hour and turned back to the waystone. Dilan, who had followed his tracks, rope-bound them there (knots on each wrist, names spoken to the stones, destination the third bend) and led him down the winter line. The ice shelf above the third bend gave way and they slid onto the road ice below it. Dilan cut his own rope; Kiran lay on the road ice, off the closed pass, until dawn, with his ear frozen to the glaze.
Rohan sees Kiran's torn ear in the passage as Kiran is led past, his eyes lingering on the missing rim, then chooses not to ask. Meera watches the choice.
Meera learned Dilan's name, the hymn and the rope end from Rohan in the hut, in a telling after chapter 9.
Heavy snow in the night drifts the lower road shut at the gully bend; the carter turns back and Meera and Rohan lose a day, now leaving at first light the next morning.

A crew meeting signal is a hand's length of undyed wool cord with three hard knots and a long tail ending in a loop, left on Nimmi's latch; it means the walnut grove behind her house at moonrise. The buyer uses it, and Kiran's crew use it too.
Nimmi says a masked buyer has paid the lower-lane runners for any crossing medicine for two winters, in silver without haggling, and some of it reached Ranu by the back road; she has never met him.
The Shilak post file lists the three-and-tail cord as a seized crew signal; Rohan has seen it in files but never found anyone at the other end.

The crew meeting signal is a hand's length of undyed wool cord with two plain knots and no tail, cut square; tied on Nimmi's latch it means the walnut grove behind her house at night. Kiran's crew use it. The buyer's signal is different: three hard knots and a long tail ending in a loop, whose loop points to the grove. Meera identifies the difference herself. Revises F204.

The Shilak post file lists the two-knot cord as a seized crew signal, and the three-and-tail as an unknown signal found twice on lower-lane latches and never answered. Rohan has never found anyone at the other end. Revises F206.

The snow costs a day that makes the night-before-the-Fair arrival impossible; Rohan writes Ila that he will push the road and reach the meadow on the morning of the Fair. Seventeen days since the cairn.

Rohan deliberately promises Meera he will not interrupt her at the grove and will not ask afterwards what was said; the rope hums low and level and Meera feels it. It is a promise he can guarantee himself.
Lower-lane runners receive the buyer's silver in a pouch tied with the three-and-tail knot, and none will say who from.
Rohan weighs that the three-and-tail cord, never answered in three winters of post files, may be the regent's bait for a man in grey, and says so aloud to Meera; he goes to the grove anyway.

Rohan's grove promise (no interrupting, no asking afterwards) may conflict with his chapter 16 vow not to let Meera fall; he knowingly accepts that he would break the grove promise and take the cold if she were in danger. The grove meeting is at moonrise. Track through chapters 24 to 26.
Nimmi's last redbark is three doses (the Dev boy's father and Kamla's two), corrected from four.
Pinku, six, is Nimmi's healthy grandson. He follows Meera to the grove with a clay lamp and the buyer sends him home with a walnut tied with red thread.
The cut-corner silver is thin square bits of Neshar silver, each with one corner clipped off cleanly by a tool; the buyer pays nineteen.
The sack of redbark is canvas bound with tarred cord, inked with a small brass assembly bell, the regent's store mark; it holds enough to finish Ranu's twenty-three untreated, with some over.
Varun crossed the Saddle eleven days after Meera, bound at the Shilak Cairn to a salt-road man, and left Garh Neshar with twenty men, Asha and the warrant.
Rohan told Varun in the post room that he carried the seal, and now gives it to Meera to hide without telling him where.
Ranu's grain sacks carry the regent's brass-bell store mark, the same as the redbark sack.
Meera carries Dilan's brass warden badge (taken from Kiran) in her coat, pressed under her left hand; Rohan has not been told.
Meera hides the seal out of Rohan's sight while he faces the wall and counts aloud to about 160; the hiding place is deliberately not shown (house, shed or woodpile within the rope's eight spans).

Meera hides the seal in the third stack of the woodpile behind Nimmi's goat shed, in a gap between two deodar rounds covered with loose bark and a walnut billet. The reader is shown this; Rohan is not told.
A high goat track over the shoulder above the walnut terraces runs to Garh Neshar, well away from the lower road; Meera proposes it and Rohan declines to flee by it.
Rohan names the cost of staying: he may miss the Fair and lose his writ to the warrant, but a hidden seal outlives his arrest.
The lockhouse in Ranu is a squat stone grain store at the foot of the village with one barred door and one slit window.

Varun promises to be given the Walnut Terraces as a lordship, with the deed already drawn, to be signed when the seal is in the regent's hand; he needs Rohan alive and the village intact until the stone is found.

Varun learned of Kiran's presence on Dilan's rope and his presence in Nimmi's house from his middleman's crew talk and lower-lane runners; he does not know Kiran is Meera's brother or that she is the Salt Fox.
Meera is chained by a forearm band and two spans of iron chain to Rohan's belt; the red rope stays between them.
Varun leaves a guard on Nimmi's door rather than taking Kiran, since Kiran is too ill to run.

A sealed regent's order ('burn the cough') carried by the patrol captain overrides Varun's wish to hold the village intact: the marked houses are to be fired tonight, killing the sick and those who tended them, who have seen the regent's grain sacks.
The lie-cold on Meera's left hand rises past the knuckles toward the wrist beneath the iron forearm band; her thumb, first and middle fingers still move.
The soldier with the wet cough who locked Rohan's cuffs guards the lockhouse door alongside another soldier, and refers to Pasang's account of the sealed order.
The lockhouse's slit window has a warped slatted shutter that lets a stripe of the lane be seen from inside.
A sentry throws Rohan his coat, the borrowed brown pattu and, in the coat pocket, his gloves when he asks, on the grounds that Varun needs him breathing.
Rohan's father once told him, when drinking, that his grandfather was found at the thaw with his gloves laid one on the other on a flat stone beside him. Rohan has never worked out why.

Dilan once laughed in the middle of his oath at the post and was given a week of latrine duty, which he spent singing the hymn. Ila once paced the family kitchen at age seven and found it a hand shorter than the builder claimed; she named a ridge 'Tamar's Shoulder' after a cook who fed her.

The grey-bearded officer wears a plain slate cloak without a shoulder bell and rides a tall grey. He orders the torches lowered; the red-moustached patrol captain obeys. Nimmi stands on her step and studies his face. Rohan does not learn his name.
Rohan's 'I won't ask you anything else' makes the rope hum low and level, a promise made while bound. His fingertips chill as his ch16 promise not to let her fall begins to press while Meera slips.
Nimmi moved the seal from the woodpile to the pot of steeping walnut leaf by her chulha after Pinku, watching from the walnut tree, told her where Meera hid it.
Meera keeps the brass button token tucked in the binding of the count, and the count was not taken from inside her shirt when she was searched.
Asha confirms the lowland middleman was Varun's runner, a thin man with a bad left foot; Varun paid her four silver a week.
Asha's crew has a stubborn salt-road pony, which Kiran rides on the salt-road path to Garh Neshar.
Varun left at midnight on the Garh road with his twenty men, expecting Ranu to burn.
Nimmi says Meera's ring and little fingers must come off a day after the Fair; the middle finger will live.
The lowland runner (Varun's middleman) is a thin man with a bad left foot who drinks in the salt-road inns; Asha has seen him at a table with Varun.
The salt road runs up behind the walnut terraces, over two spurs and down the dry side of Garh Neshar; it has not been warded in fifty winters and is illegal in nine places.
Pinku watched from the walnut tree when Meera hid the seal in the woodpile and told Nimmi at dusk.

Asha's crew tied the lockhouse sentries' hands in the three-nested-loop knot matching the juniper bundle and the cairn carving; Meera notices it (count note 'Same as cairn') and Asha cuts her off with a look.
Rohan has always read Dilan's rope end as a single clean slanted blade cut made from the near side, with no fraying, and has known for two winters that Dilan cut it himself.
Dilan sang his hymn, badly, all the way down the winter line while leading Kiran, saying it kept them off the ice; Kiran told him to shut up.
Rohan publicly states that by the letter of the law his declining to arrest Kiran makes him a harbourer, and takes the responsibility before Asha's four.
Meera writes in the count: 'R. did not reach. M. lied. Both stand.'

Rohan carries the queen's wax as a wafer in a flat tin, with a single line in her hand folded under it: 'Pritam holds Neshar for us and not for himself. We so say.' Signed Sarala. The seal impression shows a thumb-shaped thread of red.
Meera's count records her crew by marks, not names; she enters it under her own name only, keeping the crew out of the record.
The matching brass buttons share a nick filed in the rim; a clerk holds them together to confirm they are twins.
A grey-bearded officer in a plain slate cloak lays his sword belt on the grass at the Fair and stands unarmed; no one names him.
Prince Kunal tells Meera her count is 'entered' and cannot be unsaid; he does not reveal himself as the masked buyer.
Rohan says in his speech that he hanged two men under the Closing Law and one was a seventeen-year-old carrying salt to his mother.

Nimmi reaches Garh Neshar on the second grain cart the hill council allows through, two days after the Fair, to amputate Meera's ring and little fingers; she then stays nine days to help draft the law.
While counting through the amputation, Meera names the people she has carried in order and, after 206, adds Rohan as 207.

Rohan has a left glove made for Meera: felted wool lined with lambskin, cut for a thumb and three fingers. He measured her hand with a cord while she slept, because the numb left hand cannot feel frost.

Drafting takes six weeks in the guest-house at Garh Neshar and produces an eleven-line law; Kunal visits twice. Licences carry two seals, the Shilak post's and the hill council's. Ila measures Rohan's arm against the post door and fixes the rope limit as twelve spans of the guide's own arm.

The dispatches say Varun lies in the Garh Neshar cellar and goes to Taravan in chains when the passes open, and Pritam is held in his own seat. The assembly's paper says the regent's general is exiled across the border; Nimmi says Ranu will tell it otherwise. Rohan never learns the grey-bearded officer's name.
Rohan promises Meera he will not hand her to anyone, though he has not worked out how the writ will say so; the rope hums level. In the night scene he also promises, 'I will stay.'

Ila stays in Garh Neshar to finish her map when Meera and Rohan leave. They cross back with the writ naming Meera as his guide, and see the Shilak Cairn from the last ridge two or three nights before the thaw.
Gopal is the Shilak post's senior warden, grey at the temples, nine winters under Rohan; he reminds Rohan of the writ at the cairn and then salutes and enters Rohan's declaration in the post book.

The bell Meera hangs on the cairn is Badami's large working bell (brass drum bell, green at the seams, worn tongue), fetched from the goat pen by Bindu. The small kid-bell was buried with Sunni at Ranu (F173).
Bindu spun the new betrothal rope over the winter: undyed cream wool, two arm-spans long. Meera ties Rohan's warden's double hitch on his wrist; he ties her flat reef with half hitch on hers.
Rohan's 'I am not arresting her' declaration is made publicly before the wardens at the cairn; Meera has already used 'Rohan' in private, and here she says it publicly as a chosen name.

The carving of two hands on the cairn's inner face shows one broad worker's hand and one longer narrow hand, with the rope's end cut or untied at the foot; Meera notices the chronicle's 'brothers in arms' does not fit.
Kiran stayed at Garh Neshar with Ila to mend when Meera and Rohan crossed back; he was too weak for the road and is absent from the Shilak Cairn at the thaw.

In chapter 31, Meera was in the room when Kiran sat silent at the drafting table beside Dilan's rope end and answered Rohan's 'It is for the next one' with a nod; at the thaw she reads that silence as a sign Kiran means to pay the Old Bargain himself.
Roop and Chand's rope-bond was tied at the Shilak Cairn, so it ends at the same first meltwater as Meera and Rohan's.

Ch19 is day 12 of twenty and the Snow Fair falls at dawn of day 20, so eight days remain at the end of ch19. Supersedes F178 (four days) and restores F177's eight. The general rides up after the Fair.
The patrol's pass rule: no one goes in or out of a marked house after the third day without a pass (F179 stands).
Rohan's grey pattu hangs on the shed ladder rail to dry; he snatches it up into the loft as the patrol arrives. Nimmi stops the loft search by falsely claiming her goats carry the grey cough.

Ch19 ends with four days to the Fair; the road to Garh Neshar is a day for a sound man and a day and a half for Rohan; they must leave by the third day, the day the patrol's door rule bites (keeps F178, F179; discards F275, F277).

Rohan wears his grey pattu from the grave to the shed; Meera strips it off him on the ladder and buries it in the loft hay, then recovers it afterwards. Nimmi stops the loft search by falsely claiming her goats carry the grey cough.

Meera counts seventeen courses still running and thirty-four cups Nimmi must pour alone behind the shut door; she writes 'Third day. Thirty-four cups. Nimmi alone. I go.' in the count. The ash print sits on the lintel over the room where Kiran lies.
Varun asked Rohan at the post table whether his sister Ila was safe in Neshar through the winter.
Varun added the shrine to the fallback sheet, saying 'Captain-ji, you've forgotten the shrine'; Rohan had not forgotten it.
Auntie, one of Jassi's goats, was the one who kicked.
Rohan first walked the Neshar-side trail at twelve with his father's hand on his collar.
Nimmi says she has buried most of Ranu's thirty-one dead herself.
Throughout the crossing Rohan has habitually reached for the downhill place on the rope and the first step through doors, and Meera has stopped him each time.
The brass button token was stitched into the spine of the count; Meera picks three binding stitches loose with her thumbnail and a tooth to free it, leaving the spine gaping.
Crate marks on Meera's redbark drops: a bell scored through the stamp, then the stamp scraped off with a spoon in a left-handed scrape. Her page records ten winters of drops.
Rohan, bound by his promise of no more questions, stops himself at 'May I' and rephrases as an offer; Meera notes 'nearly's free'.

Book 1 day count: Rohan reaches Kothi Shilak on day 1, the avalanche and binding are on day 2, and the Snow Fair falls at dawn of day 20. Days remaining to the Fair: eleven at ch 13 dusk (day 9), eight at ch 19 (day 12), five at the start of ch 21 (day 15) and four in ch 22 (day 16). Supersedes F129, F178, F185, F189, F192 and F278.
Rohan counts Varun as buried under the gully for seven days at ch 13 and eight days at ch 16. Supersedes F131 and F153.
The patrol's door rule bites after the sixth day from the ash marking (day 18): no one goes in or out of a marked house without a pass after that. Supersedes F179, F193 and F276.

The ch 21 plan: the two marked cases take their last dose at dusk on day 16, and the pair leave at first light on day 17. The ch 23 snow delays departure to day 18, and Rohan's unsent letter tells Ila he will reach Garh Neshar the evening before the Fair. Supersedes F209's morning-of-the-Fair wording.
Rohan struck the third warden from Varun's party sheet before riding to Kothi Shilak and named only two in the yard. No one in Kothi ever heard the number three. Supersedes F107 and F114.
Rohan first says 'Meera' in ch 7, when she lies about the shelf. Ch 10 is the first time he says it on purpose. Supersedes F088's ch 6 claim.
Rohan's lockhouse promise in ch 27 is worded 'I won't ask you anything else about that rope', so it binds only questions about Dilan's rope. Refines F239 and F289.
Meera has an old burn-scar on her forearm (ch 20).
Rohan has read the Shilak post's file on Meera, which records her age (ch 20).
Kiran tried, alone at the cairn last winter, to say Dilan's name aloud and could not.
Nimmi chalks each dose tally on her lintel beside the ash handprint.
On the night of the torches the regent's soldiers nail planks across Nimmi's goat shed door.
Rohan's father, the one time he saw Dilan's rope end, said: 'Burn it, or carry it, but don't turn it into a kind of priest.'
In the lockhouse Rohan hums Dilan's hymn, whose invented verse begins 'keep me till the morning, love'. Meera tells him it is a hymn, not a love song.
In ch 1 the redbark came in four crates, all four lids scraped. Meera's last recorded delivery was seven crates left at the mill below the village.
Meera learned the lazy woman's lift at fourteen from Bindu's mother. She once counted in her head and carried eleven packets over the Saddle while calling them twelve.
The Goat's Teeth drop about two thousand feet to the Neshar side.
At the Fair, Lalit trips the fleeing Varun and Asha sits on his chest. Kunal's single word 'Hold' stops the soldiers moving on Meera.
Ila greets Rohan at the Fair by telling him he is eight days late.
On the crossing home Meera adds a fifth stone to Jassi's waystone cairn 'for the goats'. The wind-felled juniper below the Rope-Hut has put out green tips.
Roop and Chand are a married couple, bound together by the rope until the thaw.
Meera's mother taught her to count aloud ('a number spoken is a number kept').
The widow Puja has a son whom Meera promises a free crossing next run, to be paid for by the Taravan salt merchant's double fee.

On the morning of the warden sweep Meera left the count and the oilcloth roll on the top-room table, then grabbed both when the horns sounded; she carries the count inside her coat against her ribs while Rohan looks at her.
Meera knows the third empty peg on the hanging tree is waiting for the Salt Fox, which is herself.

At the Shilak Cairn Rohan asks 'And the medicine in your pack?', so Meera learns he knows she carries medicine (he found the redbark grain in ch 2). She reasons he has not seized it and cannot tell why, and answers with silence.
Meera moved the oilcloth roll of redbark from the fleece under the goat straps into the bottom of her own pack at the last halt before the avalanche.

During the bowl crossing Rohan ignores Meera's thirty-pace spacing and closes to a few paces behind her, which is how he reaches her when the slope slides. Meera notices and resents it; she tells him afterward to stay behind her where she ordered.
Rohan's post archive quotes the cairn rule only as 'One rope, one pair, until meltwater runs at this cairn.'
Meera thinks plainly, in her own head, that she is the Salt Fox and that Rohan would hang her at the thaw if he connected the two. She says nothing aloud.

Stones of the old cairns and waystones hum when a bound pair lies near them and rise in pitch when one of the pair lies. They do not say which one. They are not a truth-test on their own; Meera judges truth by the sum of what is said and by the fingertips. Extends F015 and replaces F081's truth-detector use.

The winter Meera was fifteen, on her first bound crossing with her mother, she went back for a dropped mitten past the rope's length and felt separation cold; her mother screamed. This retires the older childhood-rope-play fact (continuity F079); F080 stands.
The lower hand in the waystone carving has a cut across the knuckles, which may be a scar, wear or the carver's intent. Meera and Rohan argue it without proof.

Rohan's lie 'It's nothing' about his ribs is small in his own measure: he hides the true damage because Meera said a worse answer would cost them a day and his Fair, and a refusal would have told her the same thing. He knows his fingertips will show it.

Rohan says that sharing the fire is harbouring with no story he could tell the post, unlike carrying the packets, which he could still call evidence in custody. Meera registers that the crew Rohan hunts for a dead warden is her own, with dread.

Ch 8: Meera tells Rohan she saw a crown stamp scraped off the crates and never asked whose; she buys through a lowland middleman who sells via the lower-lane runners (matches F205/F211). She marks a round sieve-print beside his entry in the count.
Ch 8: one night's fire is five sticks; the next woodpile lies two days' walk past the Rope-Hut; the warden mess serves sattu unsalted.
Ch 8: Meera decides not to wake Rohan about the torches and to tell him at dawn.

Asha knows Meera of Shilak is the Salt Fox and puts a price on her: two hundred silver for the skin, a hundred more if she comes in quiet. Asha swears to bring her down alive. Needs an S2 ruling against F228 (Varun does not know; Asha may know separately).
Asha says the regent will pay a lordship's purse in Neshar silver and a crown pardon for her crew, and claims he will have the queen's hand by midwinter.
Asha offers to add every Shilak name Meera gives her, including Kiran, to the regent's clerk's pardon list.
A cairn stands on the rise above the Rope-Hut and hums through the slates when Rohan speaks a true word.

Meera deduces that 'three wardens' could only come from a paper written before the party was cut to two. She withholds this from Rohan as leverage. Rohan refuses to say whether the regent wants him dead or only the coat.
Asha knows the red rope is eight spans and sits nine spans from the hut door, just beyond a bound guide's reach, so Meera cannot close the distance.
Meera writes in the count: 'Three wardens, two goat-folk. Said by Asha's boy. We were two and two.'

The Shilak post's file holds a seized Taravan factor's receipt showing a crossing paid at twice the Kothi rate, while a widow's crossing with a sick child the same week has no payment recorded. This anomaly lets Rohan infer Meera's double pricing. Supersedes the 'guessing from a sum' basis in F124.
Ch 12 retires F121 and F123 in favour of F125 and F126. At the end of ch 12 the regent's hunters' two-note falling horn sounds from downslope, where Asha's crew went.

The Goat's Teeth is a spine of steep rock on the south-east shoulder of the Long Saddle: three ledges, two ropes' worth of down-climbing and an ice chimney, dropping about two thousand feet to the Neshar side below the third bend. A pair needs a day and a half, Rohan one-armed about two. Jassi named it and hated it.

Rohan's grandfather was a warden of the Shilak post sixty winters ago, before the post had a hall. He went out in a night storm to check the cairns for a lost party and was found at the thaw. The Closing Law was written the next spring. Rohan believes it was an accident.
Rohan says he has buried seven wardens and that Pritam would open the Shilak to his grain wagons by midwinter if the Closing Law lapsed.

Meera buys a second question round for both leads by burning a wet juniper deadfall branch, which is not part of the counted dry bundle. Rohan then burns one dry stick for silence about the fines, leaving twelve.
Meera's answer to what she would do if the law were gone is 'Sleep.' Rohan's silence on the fines confirms to her that he pays them.
Meera tells Rohan that at the thaw he will deliver her, so she will not kiss him. She says it deliberately so he chooses with open eyes before the Teeth. Rohan's eyes go still on the word 'me'.
Meera's count holds a page from the Rope-Hut where she wrote Rohan as 'Warden. The noose.'; at Ranu she cannot add a line beneath it.
A drover in a felt cap stacks split pitch-pine at the foot of Ranu's lane against the last wall, planted as a clue to the 'cleansing'; Nimmi notes nobody in Ranu burns pitch-pine.
Rohan has believed the Closing Law for twelve years.
Rohan's 'Until then I carry every bucket' is a sincere bound promise; the rope hums low and level (applies F149).
Ch19 ends with eight days to the Fair and the door rule biting after the sixth day, per F290 and F292; Nimmi's untreated count is 'twenty-three, no course' (supersedes F280's 'thirty-four cups').
The Shilak blockade order is written by the post commander and signed by the captain; Rohan signed it in the autumn before first snow, three winters running (ch 20).
Meera has an old burn-scar on her forearm; Rohan kisses it in ch 20.
When Meera begins to say a half-false claim aloud, her fingertips start to whiten; she stops before completing it, corrects herself, and the colour returns (ch 20).
The ash handprint is on the lintel of Nimmi's storehouse door as well as the house (ch 20).

Revises F350. In ch 20 Meera starts a half-false claim, her first two fingertips whiten, and she corrects herself, but the white stays for the full hour as the rule requires. She tells Rohan her hands cannot vouch for anything she says in that hour, says 'I want you' anyway, and he takes it unverified on her word. The colour has returned by the time they lie afterwards.
Ila greets Rohan at the Fair by telling him he is two hours late and a belt-hole thinner (measured exactly, as a surveyor would). Revises F308's 'eight days late'.

At the Fair Pritam orders the forty to hold the herald and claims Neshar owes him eleven hundred measures of winter grain; Rohan answers that his bell mark is on every sack in Ranu. The officer's spear drops and he gives no order after Tej's sword belt lies on the grass.
Meera uses the rope signal of one long pull (come, per F128) to call Rohan away from Ila at the Fair; he leaves his sister mid-sentence and follows.

At the Fair Pritam orders the forty to hold the herald and claims Neshar owes him eleven hundred measures of winter grain. Rohan answers that those are the crown's measures, carry Pritam's store-bell, were hoarded through the closing and sold back to Ranu at famine price; a hill-council man says he paid four times the autumn price for a sack. The officer lowers his spear only after Tej's sword belt lies on the grass. Revises earlier F354 wording.
Meera uses the rope signal of one long pull (come, per F128) to call Rohan away from Ila at the Fair; he leaves his sister mid-sentence and follows.

At the Fair two soldiers take Meera's arms and the herald enters her as 'Meera of Kothi Shilak, called the Salt Fox. Held pending the queen's judgement.' Kunal's 'Hold' stops them removing her; the officer has them release her after the herald is freed. The entry stands in the crown's record. (F353, Ila's 'two hours late', is withdrawn; F308 'eight days late' stands.)

Old Bhim of the hill council argues for striking the Shilak post's seal from winter licences; Rohan concedes that the post signs second and may read but not refuse a licence the council has sealed, giving up the veto he held twelve winters.
A bound rope in the Winter Crossing Law is eight spans of the guide's own arm; Ila corrects 'about eight' to 'exactly eight'. This matches the eight-span rope elsewhere and supersedes F263's twelve.
Ila measured Rohan's arm against the post door before the snow closed the road; it runs a hair over the common.

Rohan says he has not found how to make the writ's orders to deliver the Salt Fox say no, and refuses to promise it because a broken promise would strike him as a great lie. The rope does not hum. Supersedes F265's first promise.
Meera is entered as 207 in her count after the amputation; Rohan has a felted, lambskin-lined left glove cut for a thumb and three fingers.
The eleven-line law: licences carry two seals; medicine always passes; no person is hanged or held to blame for a death on a bound crossing.
From the last ridge the village roofs, the salt house and goat pen lie below, and the Shilak Cairn sits nearer, at the foot of the pass above the village.
The Rope-Hut's door nail is bare; the fourth waystone stone is Rohan's and Meera adds a fifth for the goats.

The Winter Crossing Law sets the bound rope at eight spans of the guide's own arm (what one guide can hold on a slide). The spirit limit stays twelve arm-spans (F008); Rohan says so, and Ila jokes that someone should measure the jogini's twelve. This supersedes F263's twelve for the law.

Rohan's night promise 'I will stay' makes the rope hum low and level, felt by both of them (applies F149). His 'I do not mean to abuse the call' is stated as belief, not a vow, and the rope stays silent.
At the Garh Neshar gate Kiran, too weak for the road, stands silent in his blanket with a hand on his torn ear, and stays with Ila (sets up F272, F273).
Hakam's cousin, the winter Meera was nineteen, is the first person in her count; the second is his wife.
A Neshar post stands on the road back toward Shilak; its guards pass the writ after one look at the seal.

Jassi's sister is named Leela; she keeps the retired bell-goat Badami in her apricot orchard of forty trees. Badami's big bell hangs at the Shilak Cairn; Jassi's small kid bell is buried with Sunni at Ranu.
Asha is wide in the shoulder, has a coin-wide gap in her front teeth, and wears a felt hat with a salt-stained brim (ch 10). Her second rope pair includes a girl (ch 28).

At the waystone Dilan told Kiran, 'You're going to die up here, you idiot. Come down with me and be hanged in the morning like a sensible person', then 'Wrists, then. Names.' He also said, 'I'll hand you to the road and we'll never have met.' Kiran screamed at him not to cut the rope (ch 22, 29).
After Kiran's confession Rohan carries Dilan's badge (DIL scratched on the back) beside the clean-cut rope end in his coat (ch 29).
Varun held Rohan's horse at the Taravan gate when Rohan was newly captain, and stood at Dilan's grave in the wardens' row with a skin of wine (ch 17).
Last spring Ila wrote to Rohan that Neshar was lovely and the passes would be fully drawn by midwinter; winter came a month early (ch 21).
Rohan names Meera on his writ as his guide for the crossing home, which enters her in the Closing Roll for life with winter service owed whenever a warden calls (ch 31).
In Ranu, Kamla's girl is five and missing her front teeth, Kamla's boy is three, the Dev boy is eight, Hira the weaver is about sixty, and Bholu's daughter has the rash (ch 18, 23).
Ila greets Rohan at the Fair as 'eight days late and a belt-hole thinner' (ch 30).
Chand, of the crew pair Roop and Chand, is a big, shy man (ch 32).
At the Fair Pritam wears a butter-coloured coat, Prince Kunal wears a prince's circlet, and the herald is a thin man with a brass voice (ch 30).
Revises F063: the warden report of Dilan's death records blood on the ice and a scrap of skin frozen to it, torn from the rim of an ear (not cartilage), consistent with Kiran's blackened ear rim.
Rohan privately counts Meera's first lie to him: her ch 1 claim that Jassi was deaf in the left ear and had a cold in his chest, disproved when Jassi answered across the yard. He says nothing.

Revises F060: Varun lost a pewter button on the stair and wears a brand-new brass one from the quartermaster's tin of odds, among his pewter buttons; he also grumbles of a frayed cuff and chalky issue polish. It is named once in a run of gripes.

Rohan's sealed order reads 'Bring in the Salt Fox at the thaw'; he does not know why the queen wants the fox delivered rather than hanged. The order's seal has been broken once and pressed flat since.

When Meera tells Rohan a true thing at the Shilak Cairn ('Because my brother is dying there'), the stones' hum drops half a note, like a bowl's song when a wet finger leaves the rim. Extends F081 and F320.
Bindu's wool is dyed with walnut husk; Jassi's goat-brown sleeve is her weave.
Bindu's knot-song for the wrist knot runs 'Two over, one under, the third one tells the truth.'

Rohan has crossed by writ before with the post's paired guides and seen cairn-light only a lamp's throw; he has never seen the line run so far ahead so fast. Paid guides tie for a fee, and Meera says the mountain can tell the difference.
A warden cannot read cairn-song: the stones' hum dips at a true word but never says who spoke, so Meera's pink fingertips are the only proof Rohan can read. Applies F387 and F320.
Rohan's writ orders him to deliver the Salt Fox to the warden-judge at Taravan at the thaw, alive if the mountain permits.
Before the slide Varun dropped back for a strap; Meera and Rohan now read this, with the pick's iron ring, as Varun setting the avalanche. Rohan thanked him for choosing the gully.
Rohan used the night's question in the firewood rule to ask 'Who is the Salt Fox?'; Meera answered rather than burn a sixth stick, and used her own question to ask what his writ says.
Varun laughed at how long the pedlar took to find a brass button for his coat.

Meera re-stitched the count's spine after every drop for ten winters, and sewed the brass button token into it the night after the last drop (the ch 1 drop). Corrects the earlier 'ten winters back' stitching; consistent with F052. Her match to Varun's coat button rests on it being new, brass, domed and plain, of the same pattern, with a shank never sewn to anything.
Nimmi says Meera's ring and little fingers must come off two days after the Fair, matching F260. Supersedes F245's 'a day after'.
Meera has seen the new brass button on Varun's coat in the Kothi yard (F060/F385) and tells Asha so; Asha independently saw one on the day Varun hired her.

Chetu of Upper Kuhl is a hill-council man whose valley has forty sacks left, all the regent's; he half-rises to speak for Pritam's grain at the Fair, then sits back when a woman says she paid four times the autumn price. He may reappear in ch31 as a reluctant signatory.

The officer of the forty lowers his spear because his own sister's house paid four times the autumn price for a bell-marked sack, as well as seeing Tej's sword belt on the grass. The 'And another' crowd chorus is cut.
Asha lays a page torn from Meera's count beside the book at the Fair; its dates match her own record of Varun's payments.
Rohan counted thirty-one graves and held the rope while the thirty-second was dug, so he states thirty-two to the assembly.

Meera writes her own name in the herald's book ('Meera of Kothi Shilak, called the Salt Fox') with the herald's pen; the herald adds 'Held pending the queen's judgement' beneath it. She says 'Law's a rope. Depends who ties it.'

In the Garh Neshar room Meera and Rohan have their second love scene; she keeps her left glove on and does not count anything afterwards. Rohan says 'The thaw is a long way off yet' as a plain sentence, not a promise, and the rope stays level.
Held names not presented at the Shilak post by the thaw go to the assembly lockhouse; this is why Meera cannot wait out the thaw in Neshar and take summer roads.
Badami's big bell hangs on a peg by the stair in the Kothi Shilak salt house; Meera takes it down on returning, and sends Badami with Roop and Chand to Jassi's sister Leela's apricot orchard.

Alternative to the Closing Roll: Meera could cross back as a held name in Rohan's custody, with no Roll entry. The queen would judge her at Taravan in spring, and her name and her crew's marks would stay open to the assembly's questioning until then. Replaces F405's lockhouse rule.
On the night of ch 12 the hut fire is carried on wet juniper deadfall over one dry stick, so the dry bundle falls only from twenty to nineteen before ch 13 dusk.
Meera's amputation glove is cut for a thumb and two fingers (three digits), correcting the 'thumb and three fingers' wording of F262 and F363.
After his fever broke at the end of ch 20, Kiran slept two days and half a night before the opening of ch 21.
In ch 25 Varun's search finds Rohan's draft speech, the folded writ and the tin of the queen's wax, reads the speech, and puts all three back in the coat lining without taking them.
In ch 24 Rohan counts to 160 with his forehead to the dry-stone wall at the foot of the walnut grove; the house, the goat shed and the woodpile all lie within the rope's eight spans of it.

After the meltwater ends the bond in ch 32, Meera walks past the herders' fold below the cairn, about fifteen spans by her reckoning and sixteen and a half by Rohan's, feels no separation cold, and walks back by choice.
In ch 32 Rohan guesses aloud, explicitly not as a promise, that the queen wants the Salt Fox delivered alive for the same reason she will want Ila's map: both know the pass.
In ch 32 Meera says that, as the Roll's guide, she remains unpardoned; only the queen can answer her Fair confession, which is why she and Rohan walk to Taravan together.
Kamla's two children, given no redbark course in ch 18, recovered on walnut leaf by ch 23; Nimmi gives them two of her last three doses.

Kiran, 25, stayed on at Garh Neshar after Book 1 and works as Ila's chain-man through the summer survey into winter; his sister Meera is betrothed to Ila's brother Rohan, so he will be Ila's relation by marriage.

The tower's north landing has a half-height step set into the boards that people step over without counting. Kunal's family counts the stair as thirty-nine steps ('children's count, for ghosts'); Ila counts forty. The north wall there is colder and sweats slightly.
Garh Neshar's builder, in family songs, is a drunk mason named Dev.

Ila's pace is two and a half spans, calibrated against the brass rule at Taravan at nineteen and a chalk line her father laid each spring. The tower's north face is twenty-two paces outside, and the inside room is a full pace short after wall thickness is allowed for; she allows half a span for sloppy plaster and records two spans.

The hill-council guards wear undyed wool with a blue cord on the shoulder; the Winter Crossing Law notice on the gate shows the Shilak post's brown seal and the hill council's blue seal, and a goat has been scratched in the margin by the third line.
Garh Neshar's drunk mason is named Madan, not Dev (revises F419; avoids collision with the Dev boy and Dev people of Ranu).
Ila has seen Kunal twice across the guest-house drafting table (matches F263's two visits).
Ila's licence asks the council to name a licensed guide to be bound to her at the cairn for the winter crossing (consistent with F007, F014: one pair, one rope).
Kiran watched Varun leave the Garh Neshar gate in chains in summer; Rohan's letters say Varun cried at the Taravan gate.
Last autumn the Taravan archive clerk refused Ila the Shilak Cairn file, saying the crown keeps it in a drawer she has no key to.
Dhanu is a hill route-keeper who sends runners to Kunal and is paid in cut-corner silver; his runner is an unnamed boy.
Chuni, nine, is a scullery girl in Garh Neshar's kitchen passage.
Sarn fold is a high pasture where a shepherd saw Captain Raghu.
The hill council meets in the hall of Garh Neshar under the brass bell; Old Bhim speaks for the lower terraces.
Ila's own covering note said only 'every way'; the crown's formal cover sheet addressed to the council carries the extra clause about the way beneath the Shilak Cairn, which she has not seen.
Captain Raghu fled last winter's Snow Fair (Book 1's Fair) with a dozen loyalists and has been in hiding since.

The Shepherd's Stair route-song is a child's counting rhyme ('One for the goat who knows the gate, two for the stone that will not wait...') that ends 'nine and thirty and the ghosts go by'; Kunal teaches it as nonsense so it can be carried unrecognised.
Meadow Cairn is the nearest jogini cairn, on the shoulder above the Fair meadow, and it faces south. Licensed pairs bind there because they cannot reach another cairn without crossing alone.
The Meadow Cairn's meltwater runs about thirty-five days before Shilak's in a soft year, closing to about three weeks in a hard year, according to Ila's eleven winters of thaw dates.
Ila's rope is eight arm-spans of her own arm, undyed wool bought from Lata's house in Taravan. They tie the warden's double hitch on each other's wrists.
Kiran leaves Garh Neshar at first light with a licensed pair from the Shilak post carrying seed barley (Bindu's cousins). He asks Ila to send word to him first if she finds where the Bargain is paid.

The inner letter's outer fold reads 'Open when you stand at the Glass Lakes. Not before. S.' in the queen's hand, under the royal archive seal with a thread of red in the wax. Ila sews it unopened into her coat lining.
A third person on a bound pair's rope is refused: 'A third on the rope and the mountain takes all three' (extrapolates F014, one pair per rope).
Ila saw the queen's blood-threaded wafer pressed by Rohan on the Fair meadow a year ago; the queen mixed the blood in Taravan herself (consistent with F048, F254).
Kiran has not been home since before last winter (consistent with F417).
Ila's own rope is eight arm-spans of her arm as the guide under the Winter Crossing Law (consistent with F360, F436); she names herself the guide at the cairn.
The east valley lit by the faint broken line is missing from Ila's survey sheets; no stream, path or shepherd report points to it.

The fainter east winter line runs along the points of the Shepherd's Stair route-song (F433); its fourth light, 'four for the fold', goes dark while Kunal mutters the count. Ila recognises the rhyme from ch 2 and connects it to Raghu searching the high hamlets (F429, F432).
Ila leaves the east bearing out of her field book; it is her first omission from a survey sheet. She follows Kunal east by choice after letting the rope chill build.
Ila heard Meera tell the masked-buyer story (cord, cut-corner silver, walnut) at the Garh Neshar drafting table, as a mystery; Kunal sat in on two sessions silent.
The east broken line did not relight overnight; Kunal turned them south onto the Garh road at dawn toward Ranu.
Kunal gave the buyer's silver from Garh Neshar's stores held in the crown's name, run down the back road via the lower lanes over two winters.
Pinku is now seven.
Nimmi confirms the grey-bearded officer is alive and that she knows his name, refusing to give it ('not mine to spend').
Hari is the Shepherd's Stair route-keeper, who has kept the stair thirty winters as his father did; his hut at the Stair's foot has been burned and his fate is unknown.
The Shepherd's Stair's lower ice steps number forty-one by Ila's count, including a hand-high half-step under the first overhang that Kunal's family does not count.
A route-keeper's marker stone at the head of the Stair carries fresh chalk in old hill script: 'They ask for the princes' way.' with a second line begun and smeared out.
Kunal's family counts the Shepherd's Stair's lower treads as forty by habit, unrelated to the route-song; Ila counts forty-one including a hand-high half-step.
On the ninth tread of the Stair a tread shears under Kunal; Ila holds his full weight on a hip belay and counts him as the fourth man she has held.
The route-keeper's marker stone at the Stair head hums low and level when Kunal reads Hari's chalk aloud, extending F320 to a non-cairn stone.
The Stair plateau has a west lip (a drop) and an old chain of faint cairns; the jogini cairn-light on it shows only at dusk and is dim. Ewe's Rest lies a short descent below the last high cairn.

The plateau route-song runs: 'Keep the Crow's Wing on your cheek, keep the cold hollow underfoot, past the stone that split in two, three hundred to where the ewe lay down.' Crow's Wing is a ridge, the cold hollow a scoured dip, and Where the Ewe Lay Down is a waist-high half-ring lambing wall beside the last high cairn.

The split boulder of the song is buried under a drift. Ila navigates by the bearing of the crag she named (94 degrees at 560 paces) and reaches the wall about forty of Kunal's paces off her predicted line.
Ila names a black four-humped crag Nimmi's Knuckle; it has a hill name Kunal refuses to give.
Old Woman's Tooth is a black notched pinnacle north of the lambing wall (bearing 350, about a mile and a quarter) with water under it in spring.

Name trade terms: each night Kunal gives one true Neshar name for a feature Ila measured that day, which she writes exactly as he says it; she answers one question about her orders truthfully or refuses for free.
Kunal's palms are rope-scraped and bleeding slightly after the hip belay.
Ila recites the commission phrase as 'the crown may hold every way' and says she does not know what holding means.
Dhanu's limp comes from a boyhood fall that was badly set: the right foot plants and the left swings out and round.
Ila names the small unnamed yellow star above Ewe's Rest 'Mini' after Dhanu's daughter; Kunal says it will not go on the map.

Ewe's Rest has a long main room with a central chulha and a sleeping shelf; the third house is cold and unused. The north side of the pen wall (shoulder high, about ninety paces round) has a footing a hand short of half its height, and Ila advises a flat-stone footing course a hand wide.
Dhanu's runner boy saw Raghu's two loaded pairs pass the upper fold two days ago, heading for the Hollow Moon; this matches Ila's estimate at the burned hut that they were a day ahead.
Gauri calls Ila by her name for the first time after the wall is measured.
Dhanu wears a finger-long goat-horn whistle on a thong against his skin: the Glass Lakes way signal is two long notes and one short for 'come on, it's clear', three short for 'turn back'.
Kunal has read the crown's cover sheet to the council naming 'a way beneath the Shilak Cairn' and has never heard of such a way; Ila has not seen the sheet.
The cliff notch behind Ewe's Rest is called 'the clerk's stoop' in Kunal's hill speech; Ila writes it as he says it.
Mini is six and travels with Dhanu and Gauri on the pony when they go ahead by the short way; Ewe's Rest is left empty except for Kunal and Ila.

The Hollow Moon is a wide white bowl north of Ewe's Rest with a fan of loose stone on its west side; its far rim lies about 10 degrees west of north, and the spyglass glint comes from a black outcrop on the west lip at 210 degrees.
