The Hollow Moon is a wide white bowl north of Ewe's Rest with a fan of loose stone on its west side; its far rim lies about 10 degrees west of north (about 350 degrees), and the spyglass glint comes from a black outcrop on the west lip at about 315 degrees, above the stone fan. Revises the earlier 210 degrees.
Mini paces the pen wall at twenty-two steps to the wall and about two hundred and four steps round it; Ila's pen figure is about ninety of her own paces.

The Hollow Moon route-song, taught to Kunal, runs: 'Fan on the left hand, cold ridge on the right, count three hundred where the snow goes blue, and a hundred more to light.' It is eight paces short of Ila's measured three hundred and eight.

The Hollow Moon's winter line shows only at old waist-high cairns spaced a few hundred paces apart, running north along the bowl's east wall in its shadow, with the watchers' fire a mile and an eighth away on the west lip at about 315 degrees.

An avalanche slope of about 38 degrees, wind-loaded from the north-west, lies on the east wall between the third and fourth cairns; its lower third is undercut by a spring-fed summer stream channel (Kunal put a mule through it last July). Ila crosses the middle at stated odds of one in five that it slides.
Ila's pencil leads, which snap in cold, are carried by Kunal inside his coat against his chest and handed to her warm one at a time; Ila had mentioned the breaking once to the air on the Stair.

Ila did not write the name 'Hollow Moon' when Kunal said it carelessly on the cliff, and writes it only when he repeats it deliberately at night. She also tells him the Taravan archive clerk refused her the Shilak Cairn file (matches F426).
Ila draws the watchers' camp on her sheet (fire, two humps marked 'tents?', an object marked 'unclear') and tells Kunal she has done so.

The Hollow Moon's route-keeper cairn at the bowl's north lip (Dhanu calls it 'the door') is toppled, its slab cracked, and three bell marks are scratched on a fallen stone; Kunal identifies the bell as Raghu's mark.

Prince Udai walked the princes' way in winter with an unnamed guest sixty winters ago, 'the year before the Closing Law was written' in the old women's reckoning. Ila goes still at the number and says only that she is counting; Kunal takes it for arithmetic.

Raghu's men dug nine holes round the toppled door cairn and turned its base stone face down, hunting a carved marker. Their tracks, two loaded pairs, follow the north-east fork, which runs along the rim shelf toward the Kuhl cut and a shoulder overlooking the head of the Glass Lakes. The left fork curves round the bowl's lip and adds about half a day.

The princes' way has no carved marker; Kunal states the cairn never bore one. Ila writes the words 'Glass Lakes' in her field book with no bearing, and tells Kunal she will ask for a bearing later and will mark any refusal.
The double cairn on the Hollow Moon's lip is called the Two Aunts by Kuhl-side shepherds ('they stand together and disagree about everything'). Ila writes it down as Kunal says it.

Kunal was nine when his father died. A week after the funeral his uncle Pritam took him up a ridge 'to see what would be mine', and Kunal says only 'and I came home.' He gives no more and Ila does not ask.

Ila's father worked thirty years as a fair-copy clerk at the Taravan survey office, copying about seven hundred maps without signing any, and went blind in the left eye at fifty-nine before the office gave him a pension and a clock.

Ila's grandfather's gloves were found left on top, palms together, set square to the edge of a flat stone with the fingers pointing the way he had been walking; he was sitting whole against the stone on the slope above the third bend. Her father once said they were 'like a pair set out for the morning'.
Clause nine of the Winter Crossing Law expressly makes shared shelter on a licensed crossing lawful; Rohan and the council argued it for a week.

The Widow's Ladder is a stair of boot-deep steps cut into the rock behind a frozen fall, about a hundred feet in four pitches with three ledges (Kunal says 'possibly four'). The hard pitch, below the second ledge, has fifty-seven steps and leans out. It lies on the left fork off the Hollow Moon's lip, and its foot overlooks the Glass Lakes basin.
At the foot of the Ladder is a stone-lined niche behind a boulder with a hearth and a cache of dry dung cakes under the lowest slab, where families have sheltered.

The Ladder's route-song runs: 'Count to the ledge and the ledge to the wall, / lean to the rock and let the water fall. / One for the cold hand, two for the warm. / The widow was carried down.' In the hamlets 'carried' means seen across by the hand; the Shilak post chronicles use it for the dead, including the entry for Ila's grandfather.
The Ladder's frozen fall is called the Long Braid by the hamlet families, a name not given to people from below.
Ila has read nineteen chronicles of the passes for the survey office and read her grandfather's 'carried down at the thaw' entry over her father's shoulder at nineteen.
Ila swore at nineteen to show the crown every way, and her fair sheets are audited at Taravan each spring.
Ila's omission of the Ladder is the first line she has left out on purpose and said aloud; the east bearing in ch 3 was a prior unrecorded omission, not announced.

The Widow's Ladder's second ledge has its own anchor stone, a squat knuckle of rock worn smooth by ropes. The hard pitch's fifty-seven treads are short (a hand and a half each) and fall only about forty feet, inside the eight-span rope. Totals: 36, 34, 57 and a last pitch, 160 steps in all. The hamlets re-cut the steps every thaw, and Kunal walked it at eleven.

Revises F496: Ila has read every chronicle of the passes the survey office holds, and read her grandfather's 'carried down at the thaw' entry years ago over her father's shoulder. Nineteen is kept only for her oath (F497).
A jogini lakeside cairn stands on a shelf above the shore of the Mirror, 910 of Ila's paces from the foot of the Widow's Ladder. Its hum rises when a lie is begun near it and settles at a true word.
Kunal's fingertips go numb and wax-pale briefly when he begins the lie 'It doesn't matter to me what you d--' and stops; the cold fades after he speaks the truth, leaving an ache.
Ila sounds ice by tapping an axe haft: clear ice rings, rotten ice goes dull.
Kunal's uncle Pritam taught him 'Whoever knows the way owns the people, Kunal. Remember it. Everything else is manners.' over supper when Kunal was young.

Revises F501. The jogini lakeside cairn above the shore of the Mirror is about 910 of Ila's paces from the foot of the Widow's Ladder, an estimate from a paced baseline and two bearings off the Raven Spur, worked while they walked down the basin by night; the cairn stands within a dozen paces of her figure. The storm-dark lets the cairn-light show by day.

Revises F502. Kunal's fingertips go numb and wax-white when he begins the lie 'It doesn't matter to me what you d--' and stops. The stones quiet at his true word, but the white stays the full hour (per F352 and Rule 1); Ila sees his nails bare, and he crosses the Mirror with dead-cold fingertips.

Revises F504. Pritam taught Kunal 'Whoever knows the way owns the people, Kunal. Remember it. Everything else is manners.' over supper the winter Kunal was nine (ties to F488). Kunal deliberately chose the lie as a kindness after nearly answering 'Is there?'.
Revises F505's conversion: 910 of Ila's paces (two and a half spans each, per F420) is about a third of a mile, not three-quarters. Kunal's 'a mile' is a hill-man's estimate by tiredness.

Correction of F505/F508: the 910 paces to the lakeside cairn is measured from where Ila and Kunal stand at the scree edge on the basin floor, not from the foot of the Widow's Ladder. Ila fixed the baseline at the Ladder's foot, worked the triangle off the Raven Spur, and carried the figure down the basin overnight. 910 paces is about a third of a mile; Kunal's 'a mile' is a hill-man's guess by tiredness.
Raven Spur is the crag Ila took her cairn bearings from; two ravens break off the scree at her laugh.
Ila carries a pocket watch, which she uses to time the storm front's progress across the spurs.

The storm front accelerates visibly: Ila's 'three hours' at the scree becomes 'twenty minutes to be on the ice' at the cairn after a short walk of about ten minutes. Ila and Kunal have been roped together six days.

Kunal's false 'It doesn't matter to me what you d--' is a courtier's reflex, spoken before calculation; the rising hum stops him. His nails stay wax-white for an hour and he crosses the Mirror with numb fingertips.
Kunal sees Ila's left hand go flat to her coat lining over the sewn queen's letter at the cairn and stay there while she takes a bearing; he does not ask what it is.

Dhanu's upper lake hut stands on scree above the far shore of the Mirror: split-deodar door, smoke hole, river-stone chulha, one sleeping shelf with a blanket, juniper and dung-cake stack, jars of barley meal, salt, dried apricots and tea.
The pressure seam crossed on the Mirror is called the Sleeper's Spine in hill speech; Kunal gives it as the night's name and Ila writes it down.
Ila has carried the queen's letter sewn in her coat lining for six days and has decided not to open it yet, to see where Kunal's way goes first.
Ila carries an iron survey spike as long as her forearm with a welded ring in the head, used to hold a chain; with Kunal's knife she chips sounding holes through the ice.
The second tarn is called the Drum by Neshar families ('the heartbeat of the valley', per Kunal's father).
Ila's ice rule of thumb: a pair with packs needs eight fingers of ice, three people twelve. Readings on the Drum range from seven to fourteen fingers.
Ila and Rohan's grandfather is named Warden Harish of the Shilak post (as in the outline beat).
Prince Udai of Neshar is Kunal's grandfather.
Ila swore an archive oath, when taking her commission, binding her silence about what the crown's papers hold; the queen's letter adds 'Tell no one Neshar's part'.
Ila reads the grandfather's gloves, left palms together and square on the stone, as a deliberate payment-sign, not an accident.
Kunal marks the petition margin with a day count: the hill council fixed the date at Garh Neshar for Shilak's thaw council as thirty-five days off; at this chapter it is day twenty with fifteen left.

Pritam told Kunal the story of Udai at supper the winter Kunal was nine, a week after his father's funeral: Udai showed the way once to one guest in winter and 'was not the same man after'; 'The way kills those who share it.' Pritam made the family rule that night: no prince shows the way to wife, son or friend. Kunal does not know the guest died.
Pritam took Kunal at twelve to the first turn of the princes' way at the Eye, turned him round himself, and said the rest was for a prince who had earned it.
Hill name 'Where the Drum Answers' is the long seam at the cliff foot of the Drum where the ice rings; the saying is 'Where the Drum answers, lie still till morning.'
Hill people call the third lake the Eye; the cleft at its head is its pupil.
Ila took a small brown jar of goat fat from Dhanu's upper hut shelf on the second morning, corked and bound with a thong, and used it to dress Kunal's blistered hands.
At twelve Kunal saw no cairn-light at the Eye's cleft; only the bound can see it.
Under the ice lip inside the Eye's cleft mouth is a meltwater hollow; Ila's dropped survey spike falls a count of three before it lands.
Kunal's fingertips, blistered from the frostnip, burst open on the rope while holding Ila; dressed with strips of Ila's shirt hem.
Gauri is Dhanu's wife and Mini's mother; she is practical and broad-handed, and approves Ila's flat knots on Kunal's bandages.
Raghu now has eight bound pairs (sixteen men) in the Hollow Moon, arrived in twos and threes by the Kuhl cut; they dug nine holes round the door cairn and more along the east wall.
Raghu's men drove Hari's nine goats up the Hollow Moon road; Hari was not with them and has not been seen since his hut burned.

The lower lake huts stand in a fold of shore below the Drum; Ila and Kunal are lodged in the smaller second hut with a plank shelf and one blanket. The flat hearth slab in Dhanu's hut slopes a finger low toward the door and its third corner rocks.
Dhanu's knucklebones are five polished sheep knuckles, one stained red; Ila's game is the sweep-and-catch version. Dhanu taught Kunal the bones seven winters.
Ila has written Mini's star name in pencil in the margin of her field book with its bearing, not on any map sheet.
Pritam took Kunal up the Kuhl ridge in autumn, a month after his father's funeral (beat wording). Kunal says his father died in spring of a lung fever. Revises F488's 'a week after the funeral'.
The hill name for the crag Ila named Nimmi's Knuckle is the Widow's Knuckle, for the hand a widow laid on the rock while waiting for her husband.
Ila's queen's letter is now sewn in the lining of her pattu; a loosened stitch at the hem shows a corner of cream paper.
Ila and Kunal go to Dhanu's upper hut, a short climb above the shore where the Drum booms, for the night.
Ila has a white scar along one rib from a whipped-back survey chain.

Kunal's father died at the end of summer, of a lung fever. Pritam told the Udai story at supper a week after the funeral; he took Kunal up the Kuhl ridge a month after the funeral, in autumn. S7: change F526's 'winter Kunal was nine' to autumn, and F540's 'spring' to end of summer.
The night-of-ch20 hut is a herders' summer hut on the scree above the Drum, a steep climb from the shore. It is not Dhanu's upper hut above the Mirror (F515). Corrects F543.
In the hut Ila unpicks her coat lining, moves the queen's letter into her pattu's hem and sews it in. She unties the rope for the night, then reties it on both wrists before Kunal's promise.

Before Kunal's 'ask nothing back' promise, Ila names both costs aloud: a broken promise strikes as a great lie, and each name may become a line on the crown's map. At dawn his fingertips chill when he begins to ask about the letter, and he stops.

Dhanu's runner boy saw two pairs of Raghu's men (four, grey wool, no blue cord) on the far shore of the Glass Lakes basin, with fresh tracks along the west side of the Eye under the cliff; they have seen the cleft's shadow from the Kuhl shoulder.

Ila gives Kunal leave to ask about the queen's letter, so his question is not 'asking back' under his promise and does not chill his fingers; she refuses the answer (a free silence), citing her archive oath.
If the Meadow Cairn's meltwater runs before the pair are through the mountain, the winter line closes and Ila's promise lapses unpaid the same hour, with no strike once the bond ends.
Ila sews her exits sheet and three older sheets (Stair and Moon) into the lining of her pattu along the side seam, below the hem where the queen's letter is sewn.

Kunal asks 'What did the letter say?' in spite of his promise; his fingertips whiten and blue under the nails, the rope draws taut, and he holds his hands in view and says 'I'll pay it.' The chill drains over time. Ila refuses (a free silence), citing her archive oath sworn before this crossing. Replaces F550; no 'leave' device exists.
Ila sews her exits sheet and three older sheets (Stair and Moon) into the side-seam lining of her pattu, above the hem; the queen's letter lies in the hem below them. Replaces F552's wording.

Kunal's fingertips, struck by the broken 'ask nothing back' promise, go waxy, then grey, then blister and stay dead; fire and touch do not warm them. His last finger joints lag when he closes his hand. Revises F553's 'chill drains over time'.

Ila tells Kunal aloud that the Meadow Cairn's thaw dates give a hard year weeks and a soft year fewer; Kunal chooses to push the Eye tonight for her date, not only Raghu's. They plan to rope the hard moves in the cleft, Ila leading, Kunal holding with the palm.

Kunal's broken-promise strike on his fingertips is still live cold at the skin: Ila taking his hand would draw it onto herself (the touch loophole, F013, applies). He pulls his hands back ('Don't. It's paid.') and she obeys; the dead tips are not restored. Ila holds his palm only.

Kunal's motive for breaking his promise: Raghu's four are under the cliff and he needs to know whether the crown's letter names the cleft before leading Ila in. Ila names the pressure his paid question puts on her. She refuses, noting the four have already seen the cleft's shadow from the shoulder; Kunal concedes.

Dhanu gives Kunal two red-thread walnuts as runner tokens: a boy bearing one is Dhanu's word, and Dhanu comes without asking why until after. Kunal had also carried a third plain walnut for Mini, which he ties with Gauri's red thread.
Mini, six, once asked Kunal for a walnut with a string like the runners', and he said 'when I'm back'.
Kunal's dead right fingertips cannot pinch thread, so he ties knots with his teeth and the heel of his hand.
Dhanu has known Kunal thirty years; Kunal is 33.

The princes' way route-song, taught to Kunal by Pritam at twelve: 'First the turn that turns you home, / then seven breaths and none to keep, / then the stone that weeps and weeps, / step on the wet where the water sleeps.' It ends at the weeping stone; Kunal has never been taught the rest.

Inside the cleft: 81 paces from the mouth to the first turn (a hairpin that doubles back on the left, 'the turn that turns you home'); then 40 paces to the seven-breaths slot (cross sideways, breathe out fully and take no breath until through); then 20 paces to the weeping stone (a glazed ledge with a sheet of meltwater, third step on the wet is the bad one); then 304 paces of dry gravel passage marked by small blue cairn-stones.

The way ends, for this trip, in a hollow wide as a hall whose floor slopes into black water; the blue cairn-stones continue under the surface. Too far to dive with half a lamp of oil and one night's bread, so the pair turn back.
Kunal's furthest point was the first turn (hairpin) at age twelve; he could not see cairn-light then, but sees it now as a bound man.
Ila nearly tells Kunal about the queen's letter and stops, reasoning that paying early would turn his gift into a trade; she says she will tell him 'when I can pay it properly.'
The Drum fold is a cut of shore under the cliff at the far end of the Drum, a short walk from the lodging huts along the lake.

The ransom note is charcoal on a scrap of herder's tally-hide in a clerk-like hill-script hand, pinned to the lintel of Dhanu's hut with an iron nail, Dhanu's whistle looped over the nail by its frayed thong.
Ila carries five sheets sewn in her coat/pattu lining (Stair, Moon, exits sheet and the new Eye sheet); Kunal knows they are on her.
Kunal puts the odds that the hostages walk off the ice at about one in three if he hands over the sheets; Ila privately disagrees.
Ila says she measured the Drum fold (cornice ledge, forty paces off the ice, two more rises east and west) with a sight bar from the mouth of the Eye on the first morning.
Kunal moves the handover from moonrise tomorrow to dusk the same day, reasoning that a man with a spyglass will be at the shingle by moonrise and that Dhanu should not wait another night.

Ila's lie is that she burned the sheets in the hut hearth when she and Kunal came in that morning, on live coals from the night before. Kunal finds only ambiguous ash and does not touch her hands to take the cold.
Ila's lie-cold goes into her hands first, which she hides in her sleeves, and then into her feet, which lose all feeling by dusk.
Ila mentions that Meera showed her the amputation glove at the Garh Neshar drafting table and told her a great lie kills flesh.

Revises F574: Ila says she burned the sheets this morning when she and Kunal came in, on coals banked under ash in the hut hearth. Kunal notes there was no smoke, Ila says banked coals give none, and he lets it go by choice. He finds only ambiguous ash and does not touch her hands.

Ila reasons she cannot truly burn the sheets: they are the only true record of the hills, including Hari's scratched warnings and the map she means to share with both courts, and burning them before Kunal would be one more loss for him to watch.
Kunal sat silent through two of Meera's drafting-table sessions and saw her amputation glove (consistent with F446, F576), so he knows what one touch of Ila's hand would teach him.
The Drum's pale pressure seam, which booms, is called the boom line; the ice beside it is thin, and fourteen fingers thick eleven paces to its left.
Captain Raghu is lean, ice-bearded and sleepless, and has met Kunal twice across the Garh Neshar hall; he is bound to Pasang, a grey-wool soldier of about twenty with a brass bell on his shoulder.
Gauri is gagged with cloth, wrists bound before her, and tethered by a cord from her belt to an iron peg driven in the ice beside Dhanu; a scrap of blue wool lies on Dhanu's chest.
Kunal's palms blister and split from taking Ila's lie-cold through her foot; Ila's two smallest left toes are dead.
Raghu's loud lie to Pasang, 'The limping one went home this morning', whitens his fingertips; Ila notices, Kunal cannot interpret it.
Two of Raghu's men, roped as a pair, go through the thin ice by the boom line while chasing Kunal.
Gauri turned back Dhanu's coat at dawn after Raghu's men left the fold at moonset; she found that his shirt was cut at the side and concluded he was dead before the ransom note was written.
Kunal unties his end of the rope with his teeth before walking toward the Drum; the bond still holds by distance.
Kunal wears Dhanu's goat-horn whistle on his coat (taken from the lintel nail of F569).
Raghu's men left the Drum fold by moonset, taking the boy's rope and what remained of their pairs, and went up the Kuhl side.
One long pull on the rope means 'come' and is known to every pair in the high valleys (extends F128).
Gauri brings a clay ember pot with a pierced lid, burning juniper, to the cleft at dawn.
A flat slab as long as a forearm lies in the cleft beside Ila's head, where she nearly lays her gloves.
Ila first read the meaning of her grandfather's laid gloves as a payment-sign by a hut fire at the Glass Lakes, from the queen's letter, on this crossing.

Raghu's men took Dhanu and Gauri from the huts at moonrise while Kunal and Ila were in the Eye, held Dhanu in the open water at the Drum's seam to force names from him, and he died the first night. Dhanu gave only the names of his ewes. A clerk of Raghu's wrote the ransom note at first light on Dhanu's tally-hide, and Raghu's men took the whistle off the body.
The queen's letter tells Ila that Harish went to the Under-Cairn guided by Prince Udai of Neshar, that what is owed is written down there, and that the crown has never dared read it.
Gauri has laid stones over Dhanu's body at the Drum fold and will stay at the lake huts until the thaw.
Gauri brings a lamp, a skin of oil, bread and dry boots for Ila to the cleft.
Kunal cut Ila's crutch from a juniper limb at the lake huts, padded at the fork with his own shirt hem.

The black water in the hollow is a knee-deep ledge path along the left wall following the blue stones, ending in a six-foot step where the water drops into a crack (the 'drop'); beyond it a crawl of roughly fifty-plus paces leads to the Under-Cairn.
The Under-Cairn is a vault of stacked flat stones with faint blue cairn-light in the seams; its door frame (two uprights, a lintel) carries the three-nested-loop knot.
The Under-Cairn carving shows a broad man's hand (Saro) and a longer narrow woman's hand (Hemi), implying Hemi was a woman; the old script reads 'Carried till no' plus a worn final word (unread).

The scratched column beside the door holds fourteen marks, some with signs (knot, goat, wave); the last is a warden's goat and 'Harish'. The shelf holds thirteen rotted glove pairs, folded palms together; Harish's pair is absent because he laid his on the hillside stone.
Ila takes the rubbing with a pencil lead Kunal carries warm inside his shirt; the rubbing's final word is smeared and the paper tears slightly.
Rohan has stood the dawn watch at the Shilak Cairn for several mornings because Ila wrote from Garh Neshar that she would come out at Shilak if the mountain let her; she did not say how.
Beyond the Under-Cairn door a stair of laid stones with blue seams climbs to a gap between two slabs inside the Shilak Cairn ring.
Meera is now a pardoned licensed guide, with a licence cord and the queen's seal at her belt.
Pasang walks out bound to Raghu as a witness; Kunal offers to write his name under his testimony about where the route-keepers are held, without promising their release.

For three nights the Shilak Cairn has rung from under the ground with no one inside the ring. Gopal sent for Rohan, who has stood dawn watch at the cairn since. Ila had not written that she would come out at Shilak. Replaces the earlier F604.
Beyond the Under-Cairn door a stair of laid stones with blue seams climbs to a gap between two slabs inside the Shilak Cairn ring.

Meera is now a pardoned licensed guide. Her licence cord carries the post's brown seal and the council's blue seal, plus a pardon wax with a thread of red. Replaces the earlier F606, which named the queen's seal.
Pasang walks out bound to Raghu as a witness; Kunal offers to write his name under his testimony about where the route-keepers are held, without promising their release.
The bond ends on day 35 when the Meadow Cairn's meltwater runs; Shilak's thaw comes on day 48, and the queen arrives three days later.
Ila adds a second unit to the Shared Map's scale bar: the rope (eight spans of the guide's arm) beside crown spans; her recalibrated pace is one and three-quarter spans.

The previously unnamed crag east of the Drum, above the fold where Dhanu laid his nets, is Dhanu's Rest, written in the hill hand; Nimmi's Knuckle remains only in Ila's field book, the map using Widow's Knuckle.
Gauri sends word by a boy that the hamlet old women voted to put the Widow's Ladder on the map.
The queen says she read Harish's name on a list at nineteen and never dared ask the archive what came after; her anger at Ila's broken oath is stated but no penalty is set.
Roop guides Old Bhim and Chand guides a terrace woman across the Long Saddle to the council.

Supersedes F612: the bond ends on day 35 at the Meadow Cairn; Shilak's thaw comes on day 56, three weeks and a day later, consistent with F435; the queen arrives three days after, and the hill council's pairs cross the Saddle for the council at the cairn.
Supersedes F616: Queen Sarala read the archive at her crowning and read Harish's name on its list, but has never dared read what is written under the mountain; she has reigned thirty-one winters.
As the price of the broken oath, the queen strips Ila of the Chief Surveyor's commission, giving it to another, and removes her name from the crown roll; Ila accepts it in one line.
Meera is bound to a Kuhl farmer on the last crossing pair to the council; Roop is bound to Old Bhim and Chand to a terrace woman.

Revised, supersedes F612 and F525's day-35 council date: the bond ends on day 35 at the Meadow Cairn; Shilak's thaw, and the council at the Shilak Cairn, come on day 56, three weeks to the day later, consistent with F435; the queen arrives three days after.
Meera counts Harish as going in sixty-one winters back, Book 2's winter.
Gauri gave Kunal two red-thread walnuts, one for Mini's string and one for Ila; Kunal ties Ila's to her short brass surveyor's chain at her belt with his teeth.
Kiran crossed the Saddle with the hill council pairs (Roop's crew) at the thaw, at Ila's summons, and stands in the cairn ring when the rubbing is read.
Bindu reads the worn final glyph on the rubbing as the crew knot-song sign for the day a pattern is loosed, the thaw, so the line reads 'carried till no thaw'.

Pritam escaped Garh Neshar's tower by a hidden stair behind the north-wall plaster between the landing and lower room, to the kitchen passage and a postern whose key someone gave him; he left with about six men and a pony string, heading east up the dry side.
The queen seals the Under-Cairn under day-and-night warden guard at the gap and the crawl's mouth until the fourth winter has passed.

Lata arrives at the Kothi Shilak salt house at thaw with a Taravan convoy, after two days in Ranu where she heard the story of the grey-bearded officer; Nimmi refused to name him ('not mine to spend').
Lata heard the grey-bearded officer story from a Neshar drover at the Taravan inns, who had crossed at the thaw with the council and asked Nimmi himself; Nimmi told him 'not mine to spend'.
Meera's count has a ruled blank line under 'Fair' where the grey-bearded officer's name would go; she shows it to Lata.

Lata's early convoy of Taravan wool reaches the Kothi Shilak salt house at thaw because she means to store it there before the Salt Guild sets winter prices; whoever holds the best bales when the pass closes names the figure. Her books stay balanced.
Ila named a rock knob on her summer sheets Kiran's Elbow (formerly Point 4410), after her chain-man Kiran.
The hill council voted six to three to seal Ila's winter licence on Kunal's binding condition; Bhim voted no, Chetu yes.
Prince Udai died when Kunal was four; Kunal remembers only a beard smelling of apricot smoke and being lifted onto a wall to watch the Fair.
Left on the Kuhl ridge at nine, Kunal followed a nanny goat and eleven others down to the winter fold for two days and walked into Garh Neshar at noon on the third day, telling Pritam 'I came home.'
Kunal says the hill council has followed him for eight winters, and that none of them holds the whole of the ways.
Rohan sends Ila the Shilak post's numbers every summer (snow depths, thaw dates, crossers turned back, sacks carried), tied in the post's grey cord; she calls them love letters.
Ila's surveyor's oath, sworn at nineteen, reads: 'I swear to show the crown every way, and no other. I swear to draw for the crown alone.'
Raghu's clerk is a thin man with ink on his cuff; he wrote the ransom note by lantern at first light and read it back twice.
Harish's mark in the Under-Cairn column is a square-cut warden's goat with his name in a plain hand, with no flourish on the H, though Ila's father said Harish signed reports with one.
Gauri's sister keeps an orchard that supplies the lake huts with dried apricots each autumn; Gauri sent Mini there on the pony when Raghu came.
Of Dhanu's two red-thread runner walnuts, Kunal ties one to Ila's short brass surveyor's chain at Gauri's word; Mini's was a third, plain walnut Kunal threaded himself.
After the broken promise, Kunal's right fingertips are permanently dead, grey and blistered; he signs left-handed and ties knots with his teeth and the heel of his hand.
Meera enters both readings of 'carried till no thaw' (death owed, or crossing owed) in the count.
Badami's big bell is tied to the east side of the Shilak Cairn at Book 2's thaw.
Pell Orlan is the Taravan survey office rival who would get the Chief Surveyor's chair if Ila's winter map fails; he has drawn three hills from a window.
Ila wrote to the Taravan archive last autumn and the clerk refused the Shilak Cairn file by letter (Ila stayed in Neshar).
Varun is described in Kiran's words as Rohan's old lieutenant who sold the regent every road he guarded.
Crown survey designations: Kiran's Elbow is Point 4410 (matches F633); Tamar's Shoulder is Point 4392.
The council grain slate has gone up by one sack since the last count, according to Chetu's boy.
Ila watched the Winter Crossing Law cut from twenty-six lines to eleven; Kunal argued for ten spans of rope and asked 'whose arm' when she said eight.
Ila decides to keep the void out of tomorrow's council until she knows what it is, at a cost to her creed that a map is true or false.
Ila is 31 at the start of Book 2 (stated on the page).

Last winter Ila paced the outside of the tower's north wall and logged it two spans out of true; the inside room was then a locked storeroom and only became reachable this winter, with Pritam held there and a council pass. Today's inside measurement closes the figure and reveals the void (callback to F184).
Kunal wears the hill council's blue cord at his shoulder and has an ink stain on his right thumb that he rubs when unsettled.
The hill council has nine members, not counting Kunal. The vote to seal Ila's licence on the binding condition is six to three (Bhim no, Chetu yes); Kunal, as proposer, sits out the count.
The condition: a council member is bound to the surveyor on her rope for the whole survey. Kunal names himself.
At midsummer Kunal said at the council table that a hidden road is a rope round a neck; Bhim quotes it back.
The crown cover sheet to the council reads 'Ila, of the Shilak post's family' and ends with the clause 'and the way beneath the Shilak Cairn'.
The princes' way is never written down; it has no name outside Kunal's family.
Before the council meets, Ila has already pencilled 'Kunal of Neshar' on the guide line of her licence, rubbed soft by her sleeve.
Kunal sings the Shepherd's Stair song's line 'Nine and thirty and the ghosts go by' in Ila's hearing; Ila heard him call thirty-nine the children's count, for ghosts, on the north landing in ch 1.

Hill-post lore Ila learned as a chain-girl: cairn-light that dims slowly means a road no pair has walked in a generation, which the jogini let go; light pinched out all at once means its cairn has been pulled down or a stone lifted. Who pulled down the cairn at the fourth light's fold is left open (Raghu's men or someone else). Needs a bible ruling on what extinguishes cairn-light.

Revises F445: Ila's east bearing is left off her field book at the end of ch 3 with it unclear whether her cold hands failed or she chose; her first spoken, deliberate omission is reserved for the night Kunal shows her the route (F498, worksheet trust choice 1).

At dawn, with the east line dark, Kunal says Ranu's runners can reach Sarn fold by dusk through the low lanes (no rope needed there), faster than a bound pair; he cannot go himself and hates sending others. Before dark he sends a red-thread walnut to Sarn fold by Nimmi's eldest runner.
The thirty-second grave at Ranu is a man who had nursed all the sick; Rohan held the rope while it was dug.
The red-thread walnut as a route-keepers' true-word token has been kept ten generations; a message without one is a lie or not from Kunal's people.

Ila marks nine crosses on her sheet where the salt road breaks the law (a ford on the closed side of the border stones, a gap in a boundary wall, a goat-bridge over a toll gully, six more), plus a stone-ringed halting hollow with a soot-black hearth in the lee of the second spur, where Nimmi's runners sleep.
Kunal chose the salt road as a test of whether Ila would draw a true road that could hang men; Ila realises it and he admits it.
A grave at Ranu carries a spinning top (replaces the bell on a grave in the earlier draft, to avoid echoing Sunni's buried bell).
Raghu is 'not Pritam's any more': he left the regent's service but kept the shoulder-bell habit.
The Shepherd's Stair is a door the far-side hamlets have kept shut for three hundred years.
The four men's prints share one hobnail pattern (nine round heads and a heel bar), read as issued boots from one company store.
Ila reties Kunal from a wrist tie into a chest loop for the Stair climb.
The marker stone at the Stair head hums low and drops half a note when Kunal reads Hari's chalk aloud (extends F387 and F456).
Kunal's family counts the north-landing stair as thirty-nine and tells children it is the ghosts' count.

An old rusted iron shepherd's peg is driven into a crack in the rock at about the sixth tread of the Shepherd's Stair; Kunal passes the rope behind it, so his fall at the ninth tread is a short catch of about two treads.
Captain Raghu is still Pritam's man, keeping the regent's shoulder-bell habit (reverses the earlier 'not Pritam's any more' wording; F672 is withdrawn).
Kunal says freeing Pritam may be part of Raghu's aim but he cannot say it is the whole.

Ila finds Raghu's two roped pairs' hobnail prints (nine round heads, heel bar) drifted nearly smooth beside the buried boulder, running along the north-east-by-north line; they passed before the night's drift, about a day or more ago, and someone either gave them the way or they guessed it.
Gauri, 38, is Dhanu's elder sister (not his wife); Mini, 6, is Dhanu's daughter and calls him Baba. Supersedes F534. Mini's mother is not mentioned.
The Ewe's Rest pen wall was built by Dhanu and Gauri's father; Dhanu and Gauri carried the stones.
Ila tells Gauri she can lie to anyone but her bound partner for free, and chooses not to.
The short way Dhanu, Gauri and Mini took lies open for about a mile beneath the black outcrop on the Hollow Moon's west lip, in view of the watcher's glass.
Dhanu asks Kunal to stay and guard Ewe's Rest and the upper fold; Kunal refuses because Raghu's men are digging on the Hollow Moon.

Jogini cairn-light follows keeper cairns: toppling a route-keeper cairn darkens the winter line beyond it, as the fourth light on the Shepherd's Stair went dark (ties to F444 and F664). Kunal says so aloud at the toppled door cairn.
Raghu's bell mark is a brass bell with a crossed-hatch clapper, his own variant of the regent's plain-clapper store-bell (distinct from F217/F220), so his men can tell his mark from the regent's.

Ila fixes the watchers' fire from two stations: about 315 degrees from the cliff and about 290 degrees from the fifth cairn, a 25-degree angle, at a mile and an eighth. Fixing it forces her to ink the five-cairn shepherds' line as her baseline; she draws both and tells Kunal.
Raghu's two loaded pairs, going straight along the north-east fork, will reach the overlook above the head of the Glass Lakes a full day ahead of Ila and Kunal on the left fork.
Dhanu, Gauri and Mini, who went ahead by the short way, are expected at the Glass Lakes and would meet Raghu's watchers first.

The dark stretch beyond the toppled door cairn is about two hundred paces (ninety-one slate steps by Ila's count); Kunal crosses it by memory and a route-song ('Door to the shoulder, shoulder to the pair, count the slate steps and don't look where'). The light returns at the next intact keeper cairn on the shoulder, per F687.
Kunal asked his grandmother about the guest when he was eight; his father told him before he died that she had never told him either.
Kunal tells Ila truly that he is breaking the winter rule because Raghu has the name and the rope forbids waiting for thaw.

A single steady orange fire burns on a shoulder of rock above the head of the last lake, seen from the foot of the Widow's Ladder at night; no hut or fold stands there. Kunal says nobody keeps a fire there. Ila connects it to Raghu's two pairs (F485).

Before ch 14 Kunal told Ila he would not ask her to carry his people's ways at the cost of her own. Whether it was spoken as a bound promise (the rope humming level) is not stated on the page; S7 should track it against later chapters.
Ila has never once refused a night question in the name-for-answer trade before ch 14.
Ila heard Meera describe lie-cold (hands first, then feet and ears) in the Garh Neshar hall, and so knows the rule from an account, not from experience.

In ch 14 Ila tries a true narrow answer ('My commission names every—') and Kunal cuts in with 'Not your commission. Anything you carry.' He has read her habit of exact answers, which closes the free evasion.
Kunal learned the taking-the-cold loophole at six from his grandmother, who told it as a warning and a lullaby; hill children play at it in the lanes with snow and a ring of stones.
Ila soundings on the Drum use a knotted cord dropped through a chipped hole and measured against the iron spike in fingers; Kunal drives the spike while she works the knife.
Ila's own phrase for inviting scrutiny of her hands is 'Check the work. Hands first.' (what she says to clerks who doubt her sums); not a common hill saying.
At dawn Ila admits that her earlier 'It's the storm' was also a lie, and that the sealed letter's existence is what she hid when she answered 'No'.

Udai came home alive from the guiding; the letter says Harish 'did not come home' and does not state that he died inside the Cairn. Ila's father found him at the thaw sitting against the hillside stone with his gloves on it (F490).
Sarala has kept the archive drawer thirty winters (ties to F426).
Ila swore the archive oath in a hall in Taravan when taking her commission; it is separate from the surveyor's oath at nineteen (F497).
Revises F593: Ila reads the meaning of her grandfather's laid gloves as a payment-sign on the rock shelf above the Drum, after opening the queen's letter, not by a hut fire.
Revises F705: Sarala has kept the archive drawer since her crowning (thirty-one winters), not thirty.
Prince Udai came home alive from guiding Harish; the letter says only that Harish did not come home.
Kunal says he has shown Ila three ways in twenty days; his nurse used to say 'Where the Drum answers, lie still till morning' to put him to sleep.

Kunal breaks Pritam's family rule (no prince shows the way to wife, son or friend) by telling Ila the Eye; he links its cost to his petition clause on the hill council keeping the high ways. The thaw council is thirty-five days from the binding night, distinct from the Meadow Cairn gap in F435.

Ch 17 aligns its counts to day twenty of the bond: Kunal has watched Ila's hands and field book for twenty days. Thirty-five days is the Meadow Cairn meltwater, when the bond ends; the Shilak thaw council follows about three weeks later in a hard year (per F435, F622). Flag F512 (six days roped at ch 13) for an S7 ruling against day twenty at ch 17.

Ch 17 is about day ten of the bond (not day twenty), matching F512 (six days roped at ch 13) and F517. Kunal has watched Ila's hands and field book for ten days; the petition margin shows ten strokes and twenty-five empty places of the thirty-five days to the Meadow Cairn's meltwater. Supersedes the day-twenty count in F525 and F712 and the 'three ways in twenty days' in F710.

The storm caught Ila and Kunal about an hour east of the shelf above the Drum; the Eye lay half a night's ice ahead with no roof, so they turned back west to Dhanu's upper hut above the Mirror (F515), the nearest shelter.
At the door Kunal pulls off his gloves to show Ila his dead grey right fingertips, the price of his broken promise (F555), as proof he has nothing hidden about the Eye.

The storm caught Ila and Kunal about an hour east of the shelf above the Drum. The fold of shore under the Drum, where the lower lake huts stand (F537), was already drifting shut behind them, so they went on west over the shoulder to Dhanu's upper hut above the Mirror (F515), the nearest shelter they could still reach. Revises F714.

At the door Kunal pulls off his gloves to show Ila his fingertips, grey and blistered with frostnip from the lie-cold he took off her in ch 15 (F533); they are not yet dead. He says 'That's what your last lie cost me, and I'd pay it again.' Replaces F715; the dead tips come only from the broken promise in ch 21 (F555).

When Kunal asks 'Is my family in your letter?', Ila refuses to answer but truthfully admits she asked about Udai for a reason she cannot give; her fingertips stay pink. Kunal reads the question as not idle and takes the refusal 'as it stands, not as a yes'.
Ila's survey spike fell into the meltwater hollow inside the Eye's cleft mouth and is lost; without it she cannot anchor her chain.
The ice curtain hides the cleft's true walls; Ila gets the left wall's half-width only and marks the right wall 'not measured' on her sheet.
Kunal names the garrison cost aloud (twenty men on the shelf, a fire on the tongue, sentries along the shore) before telling Ila to draw it true.

Of Raghu's eight bound pairs, seven are in the Hollow Moon bowl and the eighth pair has sat on the Kuhl shoulder over the head of the Glass Lakes for two nights; Dhanu's boy saw their fire from the upper fold (ties the ch12 shoulder fire, F695, to Raghu).
Raghu's men came to the Hollow Moon by the Kuhl cut (matches F535); only Hari's nine goats were driven up the Hollow Moon road.
Dhanu's boy ran in from the upper folds two nights ago.

The Drum fold is hidden from the Kuhl shoulder by the cliff overhang, per Ila's sight from the mouth of the Eye; the 300 paces of open shore to reach it are exposed. Ila puts the risk at one in ten (one watcher asleep, the other dazzled by his fire, no lamp), residual risk named.
Ila and Kunal have shared quarters nine times; Ila carries the queen's letter against her ribs; Kunal said 'and I came home' in a snow cave on the Hollow Moon.
Ila and Kunal stood on the Eye's ice in full sun that morning and may have been seen from the shoulder.

Ila revises her risk figure for the walk to the Drum fold to one in five (two awake watchers among four men on the Kuhl shoulder); the shoulder already knows the huts are lived in from Dhanu's whistle and the chulha smoke, so the real cost of being seen is revealing that the pair who drew the Eye are the ones walking. Supersedes F725's one in ten.

Kunal followed the nanny goat for two days: on the first night a herd boy gave him a cheese rind without asking his name, and he walked into Garh Neshar at dusk on the second day. Ila's summary is 'home in two days'. Aligns ch 20 with the beat and F636's 'third day' (S7 to amend F636).
Kunal says the hill council has followed him for eight winters and none of them holds the whole of the ways (already F637).

As Kunal makes the 'ask nothing back' promise his eyes go to the hem of Ila's pattu where he watched her sew the queen's letter; he recognises the promise covers it and lets it stand. His dawn near-question is therefore a chosen cost biting, not a lapse.
Ila infers that Kunal clipped the corners of the nineteen silvers so the medicine in Ranu could not be traced to his hand; Kunal confirms he never expected anyone to work out why.
Only Ila's mother ever warmed her feet; Ila hides them in the field, keeping them under her or in a bag.

The herders' hut's door is hidden from the Kuhl shoulder by a scree spur. Ila has Kunal keep only a single banked coal under an upturned clay pot, so no flame shows through the smoke hole; the hut stays cold.
Kunal's fingertips are still raw and split and dressed; Ila kisses his knuckles above the dressings.
Kunal carries Ila's pencil leads against his chest, which she cites as something she watched him do (F480).
Garh Neshar store silver is punched with the store-bell in one corner; clipping the corner removes the crown-held stores' mark so the coin cannot be traced to the Garh treasury or to Kunal.

Revises F558: Ila states the free tactical answer ('Raghu's four don't need my letter; they've seen the cleft's shadow') before Kunal asks. His broken-promise question is emotional, about what the crown put in her hands concerning his country, and Ila names it as his counting again. The dead fingertips and the later promise are unchanged.

The princes' way route-song, taught to Kunal by Pritam at twelve: 'First the turn that turns you home, / then seven breaths and none to keep, / then the stone that weeps and weeps, / step on the wet where the water sleeps.' It ends at the weeping stone.

Inside the cleft: 81 paces from the mouth to the first turn (a hairpin doubling back on the left); 40 paces to the seven-breaths slot (breathe out fully, take no breath until through; Ila counts seven); 20 paces to the weeping stone (third step on the wet is the bad one); then 304 paces of dry gravel marked by small blue cairn-stones.

The way ends, for this trip, in a hollow wide as a hall whose floor slopes into black water; the blue cairn-stones continue under the surface. With half a lamp of oil and one night's bread, the pair turn back.
Kunal names Pritam's family rule aloud ('No prince shows the way to wife, son or friend') and says he is breaking it on purpose; he asks Ila to correct his counts, which are her paced figures.
Ila nearly tells Kunal about the queen's letter and stops, saying she will tell him 'when I can pay it properly.'

Kunal searches Dhanu's hut, the goat pen, the pony shed and the meal chest for Mini; he finds only a knucklebone under the shelf. Ila finds the pony tracks heading down the valley path, with Mini's blanket and boots gone.
Dried apricots arrive at the lake huts by the autumn pony load; Kunal ate them off Gauri's palm at twelve.
Kunal heard Dhanu's whistle on four hundred mornings.
Kunal made the council swear to Dhanu's walnut rule; Kunal believes Dhanu kept a spare red-thread walnut in his pouch (Dhanu gave Kunal two, per F559).
A strip of blue wool is caught in the stones at the Drum's rim, Gauri's or a stranger's.
Kunal says 'I have to believe it' and his left fingertips stay pink; Ila reads the hedge as proof he doubts the trade.

In ch 25 Ila slits the side seam of her pattu in the second lake hut and caches the five sheets in the black gap where the plank shelf meets the wall, a hand deep, while Kunal sifts the hearth ash with his back to her. The queen's letter stays sewn in the hem. She does not carry the sheets to the Drum fold.
In the hut Ila's feet are wooden and only her smallest toes still answer; total loss of feeling comes on the shore near the sixtieth pace.
Hari has scratched his warnings on stones for thirty winters (F451); Ila reasons Raghu would not leave him standing once he has the sheets.
